He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is brought before the House today to remedy a situation that should have been corrected, but unfortunately was not, when the concurrent provisions of the Criminal Code were created in 1972.
In 1972, it was decided, after a long series of hearings before the Law Reform Commission, that under certain circumstances a judge, instead of convicting an accused, should be able to order and direct that the accused be discharged absolutely or on conditions prescribed in a probation order. The result of that discharge in effect was that there was to be no conviction at all.
Unfortunately, under the criminal records provision, we like keeping records on people. When we keep records, we can keep the record that they were discharged from their criminal charge. The judge ordered that they not be convicted, yet we keep a record that they were not convicted.
As a consequence, in order to get a clean criminal record, these people are now required, after five years- because they cannot do anything without a five-year wait-to proceed to the National Parole Board to make an application. Because the Parole Board is overstuffed with work and cannot get at its work, it takes a year and a half longer to get absolved of a conviction that the act says they were not convicted of.
So, we have the absolute stupidity of it all in the way the criminal record system operates. We have all sorts of people in our constituency, Sir, carrying with them a record that makes it difficult sometimes for them to get employment because they have a criminal record, or at least there is a record of their activities. Sometimes they have a difficult time with immigration. They have a difficult time generally because they have this record and we keep records of people who were not convicted, because the act says that the judge can discharge them and the judge has discharged them.
Let me read some of the debates that took place when this matter was proposed by the Hon. Otto Lang. I am reading from the Commons Debate of April 27, 1972, at page 1700.
First of all, we propose to put into the hands of judges and magistrates the power to give an absolute or conditional discharge to persons who either plead guilty or are found guilty by them. This, of course, means that the offender will not be convicted. This means that in certain cases, particularly of young offenders who have transgressed in a technical way without in any malicious sense having attempted to injure society, the judge or magistrate is given the power to use this approach instead of rendering a suspended sentence which might otherwise have been the next least severe penalty available to him.
That was the whole intent of the statute. I can go on further and tell you what the critic for the New Democratic Party said. Having analysed the bill, I found that no one from the Progressive Conservative Party spoke on this section. In the usual course, this was an omnibus bill

that covered a whole lot of other matters, including airline hijacking, and most of the attention of the debate was, of course, focused on airline hijacking.
I will read to you from page 1705 of Hansard of April 27, 1972 as to what the New Democratic Party said. Mr. Gilbert is, of course, now a judge of a court and he certainly was pretty interested in this particular matter. He said:
The Minister of Justice waxed eloquent with regard to the changes concerning conditional and absolute discharge, and 1 thought he was right in doing so, and taking a great step forward from the approach of suspended sentence to that of conditional or absolute discharge. This is a giant step forward. I was happy to see that not only if a person pleads guilty, but when a person is found guilty and a conviction is registered we will give the judge discretion to grant an absolute or a conditional discharge if it is in the best interest of the accused and is not contrary to the public interest. The result will be that in time the offence will be deemed not to have been committed.
We have here a situation where it was intended that there be no conviction and, clearly, no conviction registered. The matter came before committee. I will read from the meeting of the justice and legal affairs committee of this House on May 11, 1972. Mr. Lang appeared before the committee to explain the bill. He said:
These clauses allow the judge additional latitude where a person pleads guilty or is found guilty to discharge conditionally or absolutely. The person then is deemed not to be convicted with consequences which follow both for, say, the immigration law and sometimes perhaps for motor vehicle law in the provinces and in other places.
Mr. Gilbert replied:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to commend the minister for introducing these sections. It is a great step forward and I think he should be recognized for having the courage and the progressive attitude that applies to these sections. I hope they work. I think he is very familiar with what has happened in the past even though the judge had the power to impose suspended sentence it still carried grave consequences with regard to a person's job or travel or bonding. This may alleviate some of those problems.
That is exactly what ought to happen.
It seems to me a travesty of all justice that a person goes before a court and that court says: "You may have sinned young man but go, there is no conviction against you. You are absolutely discharged or you are discharged conditionally on certain things happening." He walks out of the courtroom relieved. He may apply to become a police officer two or three years later. He cannot, because he has a conviction registered against him, even
though the statute says no conviction. He applies for a job where a bond is required. They draw a criminal record. There it is, large as life. Even though the judge intended no conviction, even though the Criminal Code says no conviction on those circumstances, there is no job and no future. That was exactly what this provision was intended to remedy.
If you could somehow clean up a matter like this easily, it would be fine. Our criminal record system requires you to appear before or make an application to the National Parole Board. That board is busy. It is overloaded with these kinds of cases. There has not been a single case since conditional or absolute discharges were imposed where the board has refused to remove the record of these convictions. The board treats them as non-existent. They were not intended to be there. The judge treated them as non-existent, yet our statute carries them on because somewhere along the line police departments and others in law enforcement like to keep records. It is time we stopped keeping these records. It is time the judge who is in charge of the case says that there be an absolute or conditional discharge and that should be the end of it.
This bill goes on to declare that there should be a record kept while the appeal is pending, if there is an appeal from the Crown. Of course, that should be there. After the period for appeal is expired, there should be no further blotch on the person's career. That was the intention of the statute and that is what ought to occur. One does not get an absolute discharge or a conditional discharge easily. You only get it under very rare circumstances. It is not the kind of thing that judges hand out willy-nilly .The judge wants to make sure, if there is a record, he can give a suspended sentence or a minor fine. They can handle it in all sorts of other ways. The intent of an absolute or conditional discharge is that people not be deemed convicted. That is the kind of thing this bill is trying to remedy.
This matter has caused me, as a member of Parliament, a lot of problems with my constituents.
When I spoke to the committee in terms of what bills should come up for voting, other members of Parliament on the committee, in looking at the matter, declared that
December 3, 1990

they had the same problem as I had. We are solving problems for our constituents who, somewhere along the line in their young lives, committed an offence against society and the judge gave an absolute discharge. They come into our office wondering why the system is destroying them. It was not intended to do so, and we ought to remedy that.
If the government wants to oppose this or delay the vote, we ought to look at that. I ask government members, why mouth speeches opposed to this, why not support it and get on with it, and solve the problem that we all face when people come to our offices in need of help?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to speak today to this Private Members' Bill C-314.
This particular bill directs its attention to an area of criminal law that very much deserves our attention. The government has already introduced one bill in this session to deal with an aspect of the Criminal Records Act and with the period of time that a person must wait before he or she can apply for a pardon for a drug offence.
The intent of the member's bill is pretty clear. Where there is an absolute discharge or conditional discharge granted by a court, where the record of conviction or non-conviction would be destroyed so that that record does not dog the balance of the life of the person who went through the court process, it just means simple destruction and non-reference to it in the years to come. While I respect that intent, I can see some practical problems in implementation. I would like to touch on a few of those without in any way detracting from the integrity of the intention of the bill, and I believe it should be dealt with by the justice minister in this Parliament.
The first item is that the Criminal Records Act styles itself as an act to provide for the relief of persons who have been convicted of offences and have subsequently rehabilitated, et cetera. That is a bit of an illusion because the short name for the act is the Criminal Records Act. In real life, I suppose, it should have been called the criminal pardons act. When you look closely at this act, it really does not deal very well with criminal
Private Members' Business
records. It should not be called the Criminal Records Act. In fact, it does not even have a definition of the term criminal record. That is a very serious problem in an act purporting to deal with criminal records when it deals with pardons.
The result is that when you deal with criminal records in that act, or under the Criminal Code, you do not really have an idea of what the criminal record is. Is it the certificate in the original court file? Is it a secondary record that merely states the existence of a record? Is it a notation in an electronic file? Is it a statement in a police file? A statement in a police force's correspondence? Is it a computer record? Is it a secondary record that has been transmitted to a third party? How far down the line does it reach?
We have never taken the time to define that. It is an area that does cry out for our attention. We just do not know what we are dealing with here in terms of these records.
Not only do we not know exactly how that criminal record is constituted, but we do not have a comprehensive statute governed registry of criminal records in this country. We do have CPIC run by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, that does provide pretty reasonable information for police forces, but it is not the comprehensive registry I have just referred to.
I remember in my previous incarnation as a practising lawyer trying to get a record of a criminal record from a court in another part of Canada. I believe it was the province of New Brunswick. Eventually I found the record in a court in a small town in New Brunswick. I was fortunate in having a bit of an indication from the parties involved as to where I might locate the record, but it did not seem like much of a national system of criminal records to me.
How can we have a national system of justice when it is broken into 11 separate parts, and we do not have this comprehensive system or procedure for dealing with records? I submit there is a burden on the federal government to deal with that. It is an omission of ours as a country.
Two of the more dramatic manifestations of that lack of leadership and problems in the judicial system are the recent Askov decision where the Supreme Court of

December 3, 1990
Private Members' Business
Canada decision is causing indirectly, or even directly, the dismissal of thousands of criminal charges in the province of Ontario. There has been no action or response on the part of the justice minister here in this Parliament. The other one is the Charles Ng case, and it is not the only one, where after the expiry of two-thirds of the man's sentence under a section in the Immigration Act, the man could easily have been deported. But no, that was too easy for us. We let the man serve his whole sentence. Even now, his sentence is complete and we keep him in protective custody while we try to figure out if he can be extradited.
There is a clear abdication of responsibility and leadership here in the justice field in governing the interplay of the Extradition Act, the Immigration Act and the Corrections Act.
Going back to the member's bill, as to the issue of destruction of criminal records, aside from the absence of a definition of what a criminal record is, the member's bill provides a right to an individual to be present when the record is destroyed. I would submit if that is an absolute right, then the bill should be dealing with how we go about contacting the individual. If you cannot get the individual there to view the destruction, do you delay the destruction until you find him or her? I submit that some people in this country who do have criminal records can be very difficult to locate. They have learned to do that. That is another minor problem with this bill.
Last, the reference in the bill to section 736(3)(c) of the Criminal Code dealing with autre fois convict produces an odd result with the way this bill deals with that section. The purpose of that plea of autrefois convict is to provide to an accused a package plea to show the court that he or she has already been convicted of an offence arising out of the same facts, in fact the same offence. If one is discharged of that conviction, the act deems you not to have been ever convicted. The section proposed by the hon. member would prevent one from pleading autre fois convict later. That takes away the benefit of the plea which should be there for all of us. I do not think that was the intended result. Whether or not one has actually been convicted or discharged, one still has to have the right to plead autre fois convict. That is another minor problem.
In summation, I thank the member for his obvious caring about this issue and for his constructive approach to rectifying an area of omission in our criminal records and criminal justice system.

It struck me at that time that what I was doing was not only a waste of time for me, but it was an unnecessary worry and burden for the constituent. That constituent had already been discharged from any criminal liability at the time by the presiding judge, and yet his or her record or non-record in the criminal records files had continued for years. We in the New Democratic Party welcome this bill this afternoon. We sincerely hope that it will pass. Obviously no vote is necessary. We are not going to talk it out, because there is no point in talking it out if we want it to pass.

It is an absolute shame that for a minor offence a citizen of this country, even if convicted, has to wait a minimum of five years before he or she can initiate this time consuming procedure to obtain that pardon.

December 3, 1990

We support Bill C-314 at second reading. We hope there are no hitches or glitches when it goes to a legislative committee, and we look forward to this bill becoming law as expeditiously as is humanly possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the hon. member for Mississauga South. I commend him for the time and effort he has put into preparing his bill for our consideration.
Before proceeding to the specifics of amending the Criminal Records Act, I believe members of the House would welcome some further background information as a basis for discussion. In Canada federal clemency powers are exercised by means of three distinct yet interrelated mechanisms: the royal prerogative of mercy, section 683 and section 686 of the Criminal Code, and the Criminal Records Act. Both the royal prerogative, which is exercised by the Governor General, and the Criminal Code provisions, which are exercised by the Governor in Council, are largely unfettered, discretionary powers which permit the application of exceptional remedies, pardons, remissions, or respite in extraordinary circumstances. Stemming from the ancient privilege of monarchs to dispense mercy in deserving cases, these mechanisms are used as a last resort to ensure that justice can be tempered with compassion.
By comparison, the Criminal Records Act formally recognizes that an offender has satisfied the sentence imposed by the court and has demonstrated substantially that he or she is a responsible citizen. As such, the pardon granted by virtue of this legislation seeks to remove the social and legal disabilities which flow from conviction and, at the same time, to symbolize the ex-offender's successful social reintegration.
An individual convicted of a federal offence may apply under the Criminal Records Act to the Solicitor General for a pardon after a waiting period following completion of sentence. The waiting periods are as follows for the various levels of offences. When an offender has been convicted of an indictable offence, he or she will not be eligible to apply for a pardon until five years have elapsed after sentence expiry. An individual convicted of a summary offence must wait three years before applying.
Private Members' Business
As the legislation now stands-and this is the object of the amendments today-those charged with summary or indictable offences, who upon being found guilty receive absolute or conditional discharges, are ineligible to apply for pardons until one or three years respectively have elapsed after the decision of the court.
I will be moving to these particulars a little later in my discourse. At the moment, after the application for pardon is received, inquiries into the behaviour of the applicant since the date of his or her conviction are made by officials of the National Parole Board, which as we all know is an agency of the Ministry of the Solicitor General.
The Governor in Council may grant the pardon acting on the recommendation received from the Solicitor General. A pardon has the effect of vacating the conviction. The applicant's criminal record is sealed, that is set apart, and cannot be divulged without the written approval of the Solicitor General. The pardon can be revoked, however, if the recipient is no longer of good conduct, is convicted of a subsequent federal offence, or obtained the pardon on the basis of knowingly concealed or fraudulent information.
To build on this background, I believe that we should have some concept of the significance of the legislation that the member for Mississauga South is proposing to amend. With your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I will outline the impact of the Criminal Records Act through a brief statistical account, because many Canadians have availed themselves of its provisions and many more will in years to come.
The annual number of pardon applications referred to the National Parole Board has risen virtually without interruption since the Criminal Records Act was proclaimed in 1970: from 380 applications in 1970 to 8,010 in 1981 and to some 23,000 in 1988-89. While some of the forms must be returned to applicants because they are premature or lacking essential data and others are ultimately discontinued as in cases of ineligibility, for example, the vast majority of legitimate requests are granted. This may simply indicate that those who correctly anticipate refusal do not apply, but approximately 98 per cent of all applications are approved. Notwithstanding the rapid increase in applications and the high grant rate, the number of pardon requests submitted represents a very small portion of the total population of ex-offenders eligible for pardons. Although an exact number of potential pardoned candidates cannot be

December 3, 1990
Private Members' Business
determined precisely, the RCMP reported last year that 2.5 million Canadians-and that is almost one in every ten Canadians- have criminal records. More than one-half of these represents summary convictions and is usually indicative of lesser crimes and infractions.
By the way, I did want to mention that many of us are unaware that pardons are obtainable through a somewhat challenging but nonetheless straightforward process. There are no exorbitant fees to be paid, and it is not necessary that an applicant retain a lawyer. The number of applications might also rise considerably, should these facts gain wider recognition.
A sample of National Parole Board files covering the 1976-1980 period has been analysed to provide a more complete description of pardons. In this sample group of 17,700 applicants, employment was the major reason cited for submitting an application. Some 48 per cent of applicants stated that a pardon would improve their prospects of gaining employment, advancement or security in their current job. A desire to start literally with a clean slate is an obvious consideration. The desire to achieve peace of mind is another, as indicated by the 84 per cent of applicants who were employed when their request was submitted since, in a majority of these cases, the employers were unaware of the applicant's criminal conviction.
To summarize, rather than trying Your Honour's patience and the patience of this House with an endless stream of numbers, the typical offence for which a pardon was requested was a property offence and the typical penalty was a fine. Some 52 per cent of the applicants had only been convicted once and a further 17 per cent had been convicted twice. However, during the sample period more than 2,000 pardons were granted after extensive investigation to persons with six or more convictions.
Nonetheless, applicants with several convictions or who had received sentences that entailed imprisonment were more likely to have been denied a pardon. Almost one-half or 46 per cent of all denials were for attitudinal reasons; whereas a much smaller proportion, 6 per cent, was rejected because of a recent conviction. Outstanding or repeated charges amounted to a total of 5 per cent or suspicion of criminal involvement amounted to 4 per cent.
As I mentioned, the Solicitor General on the advice of the National Parole Board, which is the agency that makes recommendations regarding pardons, is equally empowered to execute revocation. Of the approximately 17,700 pardons granted from 1976 to 1980, only 2 per cent were considered for revocation and, of these, roughly half were ultimately recommended for revocation. Although pardons can be revoked because the recipient is no longer of good conduct, the board in practice has based its recommendations solely on the occurrence of subsequent criminal convictions or repeated charges.
We have before us a proposition to correct potential and current injustices. I again commend the member who has brought it forward. To deal expeditiously and more or less automatically to remove the class of applicant designated by Bill C-314 from the pardon granting process would ease the burden on the National Parole Board whose efforts would be more productively directed to the consideration of cases of greater gravity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the hon. member for Mississauga South on the impressive job he did in another area, as chairman of the finance committee. I would like to draw the attention of Canadians to the impressive amount of work done by the hon. member for a number of years on this committee, working steadily on changes to the entire Canadian tax system, to make it an instrument that will help the neediest among us. The abolition of tax shelters, Bill C-23, for instance, on the minimum tax for the rich, which met with the opposition of the Liberals and the NDP, all this was achieved thanks to the perseverance of the hon. member.
Mr. Speaker, regarding the Criminal Records Act, in 1969, the Ouimet Committee recognized the need for legislation that would ease the legal disabilities and social stigma of a criminal record for those ex-offenders who had demonstrated over an appropriate number of years that they could lead crime-free lives. The committee's recommendations were largely responsible for the enactment of the Criminal Records Act in 1970. This
December 3, 1990

legislation was subsequently revisited when examined in conjunction with the Criminal Law Review, approved by cabinet in 1981. Two important principles contained in the policy statement produced by this review were that the criminal justice system should be governed by economy, necessity and restraint, and that whenever appropriate, the criminal law should provide for opportunities aimed at the personal reformation of the offender and his reintegration into the community.
In the period following the promulgation of the Criminal Records Act, deficiencies in the system for granting pardons had been identified by the government officials responsible for the implementation of the legislation. It had become evident that not enough eligible ex-offenders were receiving pardons and that the system of application, review and decision was too complicated. Law enforcement officials, for example, were unhappy with the complicated system of having to apply for access to "sealed" pardoned criminal records. More recently, the Nielsen Task Force Report characterized the current system as "costly, cumbersome and counterproductive".
Reform undertaken in light of these criticisms would require balancing of the three competing objectives of providing relief from a criminal record to increased numbers of eligible ex-offenders, ensuring that the public is protected and creating a more efficient criminal records system. Moreover, the affected constituencies are varied and their interests conflict to a certain extent. These factors suggest that simple solutions are unlikely.
Most opinion expressed in consultations to date supports the view that the primary aim of the pardon should be the removal, as completely as possible, of all the negative consequences of conviction once the offender has paid the debt owed society and enough time has elapsed to establish, with some degree of certainty, his law-abiding behaviour.
It should be noted that the bill drafted by the hon. member for Mississauga South calls for the "destruction" of pardoned records whereas the existing legislation provides for "sealing" this information. This is a very important point, to which I intend to return. Consultations have also revealed support for increased granting of pardons in a more simplified process, as long
Private Members' Business
as there is not undue leniency or increased risk to the public.
The Nielsen Task Force on Improved Program Delivery in the Justice System examined the functioning of the Criminal Records Act, and included the scrutiny of eligibility criteria, benefits provided to the pardoned individual and access to and destruction of records. The task force recognized in 1985, when their study was conducted, that the existing method was slow-an average of 13 months per application processed; costly-91 person-years distributed between the RCMP and the National Parole Board; cumbersome-requiring a decision by the Governor in Council; and sometimes counter productive-after the RCMP had completed the necessary community assessment, employers, neighbours and relatives may have been given the knowledge that the applicant has a criminal record.
The possibility of cost reductions and savings of person-years as a consequence of implementation of a more efficient system of pardoning motivated the Nielsen Task Force to propose a "records management" approach. The task force report predicted that a saving of $2.4 million and 57.5 p/y's could be achieved under a system where the initiation of the records management process became an internal government responsibility without the need for a formal application from the ex-offender and where the criteria for eligibility for pardon was restricted, in all cases, solely to a specified number of years of crime-free behaviour in the community. This allocation of money and person-years was the total amount which the Parole Board had available for the delivery of its responsibilities under the Criminal Records Act.
It is difficult to determine the exact nature of all assumptions which were used to arrive at this estimate of potential savings. An approximation of resource implications of this magnitude could only be achieved under a system which precluded all community investigations. It is important to analyse the savings which could be achieved under the various options for reform which have been proposed. It is also important to ascertain whether the savings are for the government as a whole or whether costs are simply being shifted to other agencies, departments or governments.

December 3, 1990
Private Members' Business
The Nielsen findings, Mr. Speaker, are most relevant to the bill put forward for our consideration today. The possibility of streamlining the present pardoning process then explored was contingent upon an integrated country-wide system of record management. The hon. member for Mississauga South is calling for the destruction of the criminal records of those individuals who have received conditional or absolute discharges. I fear that the realization of the intent of Bill C-314 will run into the same problems as the Nielsen proposal for economy had it been pursued. Neither clearly defined central record-keeping functions nor a central file registry exist to administer criminal records in Canada. To be sure, the RCMP maintains a data bank that contains the records of all convictions for indictable offences. However, no such centralized system contains records proceeding from summary convictions, and Bill C-314 would entail the search for even more nebulous entities: records of conditional and absolute discharges.
Ideally there would be a registry that would include records of convictions for both summary and indictable offences as well as the class of record to which the currently proposed reforms refer. The registry would integrate the overlapping responsibilities of local, municipal, provincial and national police forces and the courts for keeping documents which refer to the investigation, prosecution and conviction of offenders.
The passage of Bill C-314 would have the effect that records thereafter: created through the direction by the courts for conditional or absolute discharges would subsequently be destroyed. Under the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, however, it might well be mandatory that the force of the amendments be retroactive. There are two ways in which the objectives of amendments as applied to existing records might be realized. In the first case, the current procedure of application for pardon could be maintained, but relief would be granted automatically and swiftly to those who wished to erase their records of absolute or conditional discharge. A "hands-on" involvement of government officials would remain a necessary part of the pardoning process. The other method of implementation would be the erasure of all records that fall within the categories in question. While the decision-making process would be replaced by the mere identification of eligible individuals, to be fully effective, it would be necessary to create the complex centralized system I
have mentioned because the records in question are not gathered within the confines of a single repository.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time is almost up. I shall, of course, continue until you indicate that I have used up the entire period of time I am allowed.
It has been noted, Mr. Speaker, that the lack of public awareness of the pardon process and the very small percentage of potential beneficiaries who now use the provisions of the Criminal Records Act raise questions about the utility of the current law. If either procedure that I have mentioned was pursued to implement retroactively the amendments brought about by Bill C-314, the intent of the legislation could only be achieved through publicity campaigns: in one case, to educate the sizable number of Canadians that speedy relief had become available; and in the other, to notify those who might even be unaware of the existence of a negative record, that all had been forgiven.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am sure I will have an opportunity to get back to this subject again, and I should be glad to lay the last part of my speech on the table as an addition to this debate.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL RECORDS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join my colleagues in participating in this debate. I must tell you that, when the Criminal Records Act was passed, about 20 years ago, it was felt that the consequences of a verdict of guilty which resulted in an absolute or conditional discharge should be dealt with as if a criminal record had been created, although no conviction was registered.
At the time, this process was considered necessary to ensure that information pertaining to conditional or absolute discharges could be identified and sealed in those cases where pardons were requested and subsequently granted. It is realized today, however, that the purpose of a discharge is to be less detrimental to the offender than if no discharge was granted. This decision is made by a judge having regard for the nature of the offence, the circumstances surrounding its commission and whether the offender deserves this special treatment.
One can argue that the provisions of the current legislation that create the necessity of applying for a pardon for a crime that has not resulted in a conviction, have also created an anomaly which should be rectified. And this position, Mr. Speaker, is ably put forward by the Member for Mississauga South through the Bill before us to-day for second reading.
December 3, 1990

It is my belief that in the absence of demonstrable harm to public safety, a pardon should be considered as a common procedure which follows a specified amount of time after a discharge has been granted. That this relief would be of direct benefit to those individuals whose reputations would otherwise be compromised is beyond question, Mr. Speaker. In addition, this procedure could result in a saving of resources for the National Parole Board which is responsible for advising the Solicitor General in regard to granting pardons.
It must be noted, however, that 80 per cent of applicants for pardons have more than one entry on their criminal record, which might, therefore, include a summary conviction, for example, as well as a discharge. The separation of the charges and identification of relevant offences to be dealt with would involve considerable time and a sophisticated records retrieval system. It might be anticipated that greater demands on the officials charged with the investigations prompted by applications for pardon-the RCMP, for the most part-would be increased substantially.

speechtext: Indeed, Mr. Speaker, yesterday I formally announced that no later than tomorrow the government leader will consult with my friend to follow up on the propositions I made public precisely to look into the serious problem of the paralysis flowing from section 38 of the Constitution Act, 1982. The question is: Why are they required?
Right on.

On June 9, when we signed the Meech Lake Accord at the Conference Centre, Premier Bourassa said that with the 1981 Constitution Quebecers were part of a legal Constitution but, with the conclusion of the Meech Lake Accord, Quebecers for the first time felt they were part of a real Constitution and a real country. Those were very important and significant times: a commitment by the government of the province of Quebec and its premier to profound Canadian unity.
This was dashed a few days later because some people believed the statement by Mr. Chretien that Meech Lake could be rejected without consequences. His shortsighted partisanship prevented him from endorsing Meech Lake. We as Canadians have to work hard now to maintain the unity of Canada that he placed-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister is aware of the serious allegations made by his former industry minister regarding a secret deal struck with Washington to increase the value of the Canadian dollar in order to get a free trade agreement. The Minister of Finance disagrees with this.
If there was no such deal, why has the value of the Canadian dollar risen so dramatically since the free trade agreement was signed? Will the Prime Minister move today to drop the value of the Canadian dollar so that Canadian companies can compete on a level playing field?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commented publicly yesterday on that. I said that the statement was absurd speculation, but it is simply also not true.
I would remind my hon. friend that Mr. Stevens was basing his speculative comments on a conversation that he had with a man who was not involved in the negotiations and a conversation that was held some two years before the final negotiations were completed.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has said that the allegations are untrue, but the policy outcome is the same.
The solution to Canada's current economic problems, including its deficit and inflation, lies in improving Canada's international competitiveness. Yet this government persists in a high interest rate policy, which drives up the Canadian dollar, which in turn reduces our ability to compete, especially with the United States.
How can the government claim to be making Canada competitive when its own policies are at the root of the problem?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend is saying that we should have ignored the inflationary pressures that have clearly been in the economy over the last three years, I do not know what he thinks that would do to our competitive position.
What would have happened had we ignored the inflationary problem as has been the case, as an example, with the United Kingdom? We both had an inflation rate at about the same level in 1988. Its most recently has been just short of 11 per cent; ours has been in the 4 per cent range for a number of months now.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance as well who has denied the allegation of his former cabinet colleague that there was a secret deal with the United States to boost the value of the Canadian dollar in connection with the free trade agreement.
December 3, 1990

Would the Minister of Finance not agree that it is the U.S. trade balance which has improved while the Canadian trade balance has deteriorated; that it is American goods that have become less expensive while Canadian goods have become more expensive; and that in fact such results of the free trade agreement and this government's monetary policy, that is the high dollar, have the characteristics of a smoking gun with which Canada has shot itself in the foot?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it surprises me that my hon. friend would attach such significance to a speculative statement made by someone who was not at the table.
Simon Reisman, the number one trade negotiator, has said on a number of occasions that there was no such deal and no such understanding. Gordon Ritchie, the number two man in the negotiations said exactly the same thing. Derek Burney, who was present at the final negotiations, within the last few months has made the same statement also. I do not know where my hon. friend is getting the support for the deal that he is alleging was made.

Too
much, Mr. Speaker. Today, StatsCan reports that a composite leading indicator has dropped for the eighth consecutive month, this time at the accelerated rate of one-half of a percentage point. Thus, we have one more indicator confirming what so many Canadian workers know: that the country has been plunged into a recession by its own government.
If there was no deal with United States to keep the dollar high, what possible explanation can there be for this government's refusal to change a policy that is a cause of a national economic crisis? Why not lower interest rates? Why not lower the value of the dollar? Why not put Canadians back to work? Why not look after the long-term interests of the economy of this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what we have been doing. Interest rates have come down two percentage points over the last few months as a reflection of the weakness in the economy.
Oral Questions
I call my hon. member's attention to the fact that there have been increasing inflationary pressures. They are still in the economy and have been there since the third quarter of this year. If we ignore them, we will go back to the same sort of problem that we had in 1970s and early 1980s when governments ignored the problem.
Inflation surged from about 5.5 per cent in the mid-seventies to 13 per cent in 1981. This resulted in interest rates that were in the 21, 22, 23 per cent range. Unemployment in some parts of the country was in excess of 25 per cent.
That is what we are trying to avoid with the policies we have been following. We have been able to control the rate of inflation. We have a healthier economy today going into a recession than was the case in 1981-82. Certainly it is the case with the United Kingdom.

December 3, 1990

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in the debate on Motions Nos. 17 and 30 of my colleague and good friend, Mrs. Finestone. Basically the amendments to Bill C-40 advocate maintaining the CBC role as promoter of national unity. This is clear enough, simple enough and very important.
Bill C-40 now before the Elouse and as proposed by the government cancels this mandate, this mission given to the CBC in 1968. Members will recall that in 1968 Parliament saw fit to include these words in the mandate or mission, namely that the CBC "-should contribute to the development of national unity and provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity".
Mr. Speaker, the deletion of these words stems from recommendations contained in the 1986 Caplan-Sauva-geau report and in the 1987 report of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. Both commissions were concerned that this section might prevent the CBC from ensuring that programming would fairly and faithfully reflect Canada's various cultural, social, political, economic and linguistic realities.
Hon. members will recall that former CBC President Pierre Juneau did not feel that the words "national unity" had created problems during the many years he headed the corporation.
The Canadian Radio-Television and Communications Commission, CRTC for short, also said that the interpretation given to this expression had never prevented nor thwarted a political debate where all views were heard.
At a time when Canada is facing serious challenges- the post-Meech situation, free trade, inter-regional rivalries; remember what happened last summer in Oka and the important role which some people say the CBC played in these sad incidents-we feel it has become ever more urgent and important that the public radio and television network take part in and contribute to the promotion of national unity.
All regions, all social partners must work together to build our country's identity. A few years ago, Parliament voted massively in favour of a resolution to promote Canada's linguistic duality. Not long ago, it also voted in favour of a bill to protect and promote language minorities in this country: Anglophones in Quebec as well as Francophones outside Quebec.
Why should it now deliberately decide to withdraw one of the tools that helped to achieve these objectives? National unity and Canada's linguistic duality should not be relegated to the realm of good intentions. They should be defined and involve firm commitments and concrete action. To remove from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's mission its mandate to promote national unity would, in our opinion, remove part of its soul, of what sets it apart from other public networks.
Some people claim, and I am one of them, that broadcasting has done as much for this country's unity and cohesion in the 20th century as the railways did in the 19th century. This has been the century of communications. We in Canada have become experts in communications. Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure this afternoon to be able to speak to Bill C-40, dealing with CBC communications.
In 1968 the Broadcasting Act required that the CBC contribute to the development of national unity. What we are concerned about in particular in this debate this afternoon is the fact that Bill C-40 drops the CBC's 1968 mandated role to contribute to national unity and provide for continuing expression of Canadian identity.
Across this country there are hundreds of thousands of people who listen CBC radio and television broadcasts regularly. Among those many hundreds of thousands of people, there are thousands who reside in my riding of Northumberland. Many of them have expressed to me their deep concern about the cutbacks the government has imposed on the CBC. In fact, since 1984 the government has cut CBC's parliamentary grants by over $240 million, which includes severe reductions to CBC technology as well.
Many people in my riding come from rural areas. They need to be kept in communication with the reality of this country. Some of them, those who reside in the more urban areas, have the benefit of cable television into their homes. One of the problems with the particular bill in front of us is the fact that it does not say that those who transmit by cable into homes across this country are subject to the same regulations as individual broadcasters. Individual broadcasters are subject to a percentage of Canadian content, and that content has to be accessible.

Through the cable system, depending on what area the system is going into and the type of programming, sometimes those who subscribe to cable broadcast have to use expensive and more sophisticated technologies to receive. It is important that cable broadcasters be subject to the same provisions as individual broadcasters. Also it is important that those who subscribe not be subject to having to purchase high cost technology in order to receive Canadian content.
Since this government came into being the Canadian public has been alarmed with the many ways in which disunity has been imposed upon the country. We recognize that the CBC, our national communications system, is one of the most important factors in uniting this country and keeping it together. We have seen the erosion of other national communications systems which have contributed to an unacceptable regionalization of Canada.
The 1968 bill respecting the Broadcast Act supported contributing to the development of national unity. It in no way prevented the CBC from focusing on particular regional issues, whether it were issues that concerned the economy on the east coast or the west coast, whether it was industrial concerns in the mid-provinces of Canada, Quebec and Ontario, or whether it was northern programming. We all learned and grew to appreciate much more what Canada stood for, by seeing either news broadcasting or situation programming that showed what life was in the diverse regions that make Canada one.
There is no reason that we should drop this particular focus and role for the CBC in the present Broadcasting Act. This is all the more reason that at the present time in Canada, when we are suffering from extreme pressures of national breakdown, we should be concerned about the development of national unity. If ever there was a time when that was important, that time is now. This is no time to be ruling out the importance of developing national unity.
Some of the programs and agencies of the CBC which contribute to the national unity are not protected and mandated through this legislation, Bill C-40. In particular, as other members of Parliament have raised, it is my concern that the northern service, the all-news service that we now have, Newsworld, our parliamentary channel, and Radio Canada International will no longer be mandated and protected specifically in legislation. When we see the enormous cutbacks that CBC has experienced and hear suggestions that it is special programs and agencies such as Radio Canada International and the

Whereas when I was teaching in Ucluelet many years ago, the kids in my class knew far more about what was happening in Los Angeles, the American political system, and American culture and music than about what was happening in Canada. As residents of the far west coast, they did not receive Canadian programming. They were too remote from Canadian centres to receive Canadian radio and television programming.
It is a serious problem. If we drop the commitment to national unity, does this mean that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation can give up its obligation of locating

translators and stations in remote communities on the west coast of Vancouver Island? I can tell you one thing, Mr. Speaker, that is not what people on the west coast of Vancouver Island want. If the government abandons as an objective of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the objective of retaining and promoting national unity, that is exactly the fear that the people on the west coast of Vancouver Island have, that they are going to lose CBC services and end up hearing the radio stations of the west coast of the United States and Mexico. When I look at a community such as the one I live in which is Port Alberni in central Vancouver Island, it is surrounded by mountains. These are things that are done as part of a national obligation to make sure that this country holds together.

I would like to bring the attention of the House to simply the matter of regulation of cable distribution systems within Canada and make a plea for the emphasis of the

national interest being pursued when the regulation of cable systems is brought forward.
Let me give the House a couple of examples. First of all, with respect to the nature of the channels that are provided on basic cable service, many of us, certainly in the urban areas of Canada, paying a basic fee, receive a certain cable service. At the moment it is up to the cable companies to decide the nature of the programming that is going to be provided in that basic service.
It seems to me that the CRTC in pursuing the national interest ought to require that very careful consideration be given to the nature of the basic cable service in Canada. Clearly, Canadian channels, local stations as well as national networks need to receive first-run priority in the basic cable service everywhere in Canada. Clearly, Canadians also want the service of the three networks from the United States, together with public broadcasting. That is certainly within the band of the basic cable service. However, in addition to those, any other non-Canadian services surely should be looked at from the point of view of what national interest is being served.

I would also like to speak briefly about the amendment that would restore to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation a mandate to contribute to national unity, shared national consciousness and identity.
This point is of profound importance. I do not think that there is a Canadian who would say that since 1984, when this government was elected, that national unity has been enhanced or improved in any degree. In fact, what we face is probably the greatest crisis of national unity in our history.
The Prime Minister is quoted as having said: "Everything that we have accomplished as a country can be traced back to our sense of national purpose, to our national unity". If we think back over the great accomplishments of the last 123 and a half years, there are many. All of them relate to this sense of national purpose, whether it is the founding of the country in the first place by the Fathers of Confederation, or the construction of the CPR that brought together the extremities of the country.
The establishment of the CBC itself was an expression of national purpose. Now, we have the very idea that this part of the CBC's mandate would be stripped from it. Surely, with the climate of division, strife, anger and frustration that we have in the country at the present moment, this is not the time to reduce any measure that we have at our disposal to promote national unity.
I do not say this lightly. The minister made the comment in the past that giving a national unity mandate to a broadcasting system is somewhat perilous in a democracy. I understand what he is saying. Particularly in the reporting of news and currents events, it can be difficult to say the least, to say that we want to convey a certain puqrose in the broadcasting of news and current events coverage.

In making that kind of provocative statement, which should be denounced not only here but across the land, he set the tone for national division that is tearing our country apart.
Now is not the time to be stripping our national broadcasting authority of its power and its responsibility with respect to national unity. Now is the time to be building it up. Now is the time for Canadians to recognize at this moment what it is that they have that is so important and so valuable. As members of Parliament we all know that there are hundreds of thousands of people around the world wanting to come to Canada. What we have here is precious. What we need is a modern broadcasting vehicle to help Canadians remember and understand the uniqueness of what we have, the importance of it, the values that we share in common as Canadians. That is what the CBC should be doing. Its mandate must not be changed.

I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak to this very important Bill C-40 respecting the CBC and the issue of national unity.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the House for giving unanimous consent for me to present the motions that had been submitted by my colleague. We feel these amendments are extremely important in strengthening the intent of the broadcast bill.
Motion No. 18 reads:
That Bill C-40 be amended in clause 3 by adding immediately after line 9 at page 6 the following:
"(o) broadcasting services reflecting aboriginal cultures and representative native languages shall be provided where numbers warrant;".
Motion No. 20 also states that the proposed legislation be amended. These motions are intended, as I mentioned, to strengthen aboriginal broadcasting provisions in Bill C-40. The bill states that "programming that reflects the aboriginal cultures of Canada should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system as resources become available".
However, this bill gives little priority to the communications difficulties of Canada's aboriginal communities. As the Canadian Broadcasting League noted before the committee on Bill C-136, the government's proposal "gives provision of broadcasting services for aboriginal people, no priority at all".
The government's proposal reflects its basic lack of support for aboriginal communications in Canada. The most recent budget singled out aboriginal communications societies for particular attack and I want to cite some specific examples.
The Northern Native Broadcast Access Program, which was established in 1983, has been repeatedly cut by this government. The program was created to ensure that northern native people have fair access to distribution systems to maintain their cultures and languages, that programming relevant to native concerns be produced and that northern native representatives be consulted regularly by government agencies. In fact the Northern Native Broadcast Access Program funds over 13 communications societies. Those societies have a significant impact on the communications of our native peoples up north.
When it was created, this program was given a budget of some $40 million over four years. However, the government has cut this in 1985 and in 1986 to reduce the four-year payment to only $33.7 million. In 1987-88, 1988-89 and 1989-90 funding was cut and frozen. In the budget this year, the government again took the hatchet to the program and cut it back to $11.3 million. This represents a cutback of some 15 per cent. This was done to a program which, according to the Nielsen task force report, shows promise as an effective tool for meeting special native broadcast needs and should be considered.
The government also cut the aboriginal friendship centre by some 6.8 per cent, the Native Communications Program by 100 per cent and the Aboriginal Representa-
December 3, 1990

tive Organization Program by some $2.5 million. We submit to you that this constitutes a virtual attack on the cultural expression of aboriginal peoples at the worst possible time.
The approach reflected in the amendments before the House at this time are much more positive than those found in the currently proposed bill. It states that broadcasting services, not just programming, shall be provided in Canada. In doing so, the amendments adopt the language found in the standing committee report which was supported by all parties and in fact included a majority of Conservative members. The amendments would ensure that aboriginal peoples have access, whether it be in the north or the south, to broadcasting services that they themselves control. This reflects comments made before the Bill C-136 committee by the Wawatay Native Communications Society when they noted the importance of having a native communications system in the north.
We need a new broadcasting policy that meets the concerns, objectives, and aspirations of aboriginal peoples, not only in the north, but in virtually all parts of Canada. The inclusion of this amendment we think would be a positive step along the road.
As the standing committee recognized in its unanimous report, there could be no way of underestimating the importance of broadcasting on the future of aboriginal communities. The communications media are essential to the preservation of the cultural heritage of Canada's aboriginal peoples. Broadcasting policy cannot ensure the survival of native languages. We recognize that, but it can and should play a key and fundamental role in helping to mitigate the threats that currently exist with regard to native cultures. I urge all members of the House to consider and support these recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to address a few remarks to the matter of aboriginal communications.
It comes as no surprise when I say that aboriginal people in Canada feel alienated. They feel left out of so many of the important affairs and matters in the country.
Government Orders
I can go back just a few weeks or months and relate what happened at places like Oka and Chateauguay last summer. These were very disturbing and traumatizing events and for the first time in a long period Canadians got some sense of native grievances in the country. These grievances have run extremely deep for centuries. It is little wonder that we had the kind of blow-up or explosion in the province of Quebec last summer.
It seems to me that one way to deal with aboriginal grievances is to address the matter of communications in a very serious way. There is no doubt in my mind that Bill C-40 in no way gives any kind of priority to aboriginal language broadcasts.
I cannot think of anything that is more alienating or traumatizing than to never see one's own culture, values or life styles reflected in mainstream communications around one. Can you imagine if you turned on a radio or television set and never heard anyone speak in your own language? Perhaps you did not see anyone carry out the kind of work that you carry out, speak the kind of language that you speak, or express the kinds of values that you embrace. Can you imagine that if almost everything you saw on the television screen, almost everything you heard on the radio was kind of foreign. Can you imagine how out of place you would feel, how alienated? It would be as if you had travelled to a foreign land, some land far away with a strange and rather foreboding culture, a landscape, where you really did not feel you belonged. Yet, I would submit that that is how many of our aboriginal people feel today.

The motion would amend clause 3(o) of the bill. That clause now reads:
3.(1) II is hereby declared as the broadcasting policy for Canada that
(o) programming that reflects the aboriginal cultures of Canada should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system as resources become available for the purpose;
My colleague's amendment would add "representative native languages should be provided" to this clause.
This amendment is consistent with the recommendations of the 1986 report of the task force on broadcasting policy, also known as the Caplan-Sauvageau report. That report recommended that:
The Broadcasting Act should affirm the right of native peoples to broadcasting services in aboriginal languages considered to be representative where numbers warrant and to the extent public funds permit.
It went on to say that the term "representative" was used to suggest broadcasting service in the dominant aboriginal dialects of those aboriginal people concerned with the preservation of their language.
When the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture examined the task force report in 1987, it supported this recommendation.
The standing committee, in its sixth report to the House in May of 1987, noted that the aboriginal peoples have a special status in Canada, a fact recognized in the Canadian Constitution.
They commented that in recent years, the policies of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission had encouraged and promoted native broadcasting. They concluded that the inclusion of a provision regarding broadcasting in representative native languages in a new Broadcasting Act would therefore be consistent with recent policy initiatives.
Accordingly, the committee recommended, and I quote:
The Broadcasting Act would include the right of aboriginal peoples to broadcasting services in representative native languages, where numbers warrant and as public funds become available.

Our languages are fragile. The threat of extinction is far more real and pressing for aboriginal languages than for any other language in this country.

The people in Canada who speak aboriginal languages number in the thousands, the hundreds and sometimes the tens, depending on the language.

Our mother country is Canada. We are from here. We are of here. There is no other place in this world where we can go and communicate in our languages and be understood.

The rest have individual speakers and once they die, that is it. The aboriginal languages are indigenous to this country. There is nowhere to go to revitalize these languages and bring them back. It is truly a loss to what Canada's history should be and what Canadian heritage is all about.
The goal of Canada's aboriginal people is to participate equally in the economic, social, political and cultural life of Canada. They recognize the need to reinforce their cultural identities. That is why language is so important. We know that, because the major political battles in the last 20 years have been won over language rights or linguistic rights.
What does a person hold dearer to his heart than the way he or she thinks? The psychology of that person is reflected in the language he or she speaks and in the particular ideas put forward.
You think in your own language first. If you are a French speaker, you do not think in English; you think en frangais. If you are an aboriginal language speaker, you think in your language first. Those ideas that are prominent are those values and principles which you are raised with and which the language you have learned has taught you all of your life. It is the means of transmitting the uniqueness of the culture of aboriginal peoples.
In the north we say that language is simply about understanding one another. If we understand the importance of another person's language, we understand why it is so important to that person to be able to communicate in that language, why language is held so dear, and why it is a true reflection of that person's culture. We have gone to great lengths to ensure that we accommodate what is important to enhance the quality of life.
The north is the model of the promotion of languages. There are nine official languages in the Northwest Territories. If you were to visit the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories, Mr. Speaker, you would find that the majority of MLAs are native and that the proceedings are being simultaneously translated into seven aboriginal languages, French, and English. This service is unique in North America and is worth preserving.
I want to take a few minutes to explain the cultural linguistic groups in the Northwest Territories. The Dene, which means people in our tradition, are comprised of several groups of people depending on where they live, each with their own dialect. The Chippewan, the Dog Rib, the Loucheux each has aboriginal culture which is really quite distinct from one another. Inuit means people in Inuit, the language of a people inhabiting the circumpolar world from Siberia to Greenland. There are three major dialects of Inuit languages. They are the Inuvialuktun, Innuinuktun, and Inuktitut. The Inuit

Mr. Speaker, I want to confine my remarks to the matter of priority carriage. With your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I shall be moving an amendment at the close of my remarks. I will not be talking very long, but I want to point this out.
Television has certainly changed a lot in the last 20 to 30 years and it certainly has changed since the 1968 Broadcasting Act. Every facet of television has changed since 1968 and certainly its delivery.
I can remember when television first came to southern Manitoba where I grew up. It was 1955. We got our first television service which consisted of one channel, the Canadian Broadcasting Television Network. That was it. In fact, the first year or two the service was pretty snowy. It was quite difficult at times to see the images on the screen. The images looked more like ghosts than they did like human beings. That was television in its infancy, in its embryonic stage. Certainly, television has come a long way since 1955 when it was first delivered to the southern part of Manitoba.
At that time, one did not have to worry about priority of carriage. All you could get was one channel, one simple service. We did not have to worry about priority.
After I had taken up a radio and television career, I moved to the city of Winnipeg. At that time, there were only two channels, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation network and CTV, which was really in its infancy in 1960. After that came a private television station and then somewhat after that came the cable services and, of course, with the cable services came the American broadcasting services, Global, and so on.
December 3, 1990

Today, we have a wide range of television services. This brings us to this matter of what is called priority of carriage. We just cannot ignore what is being served up first on the television screen. Television technology is changing so rapidly that even things like tiers are rapidly fading from our vocabulary. At one time, our television sets started at channel 2 and went up to channel 13. Now, with the new technology, they go up to about channel 99.
It seems to me, and certainly on this side of the House, that there should be a priority given to certain services. In our opinion, the first priority should go to public television services, publicly funded, publicly supported television services. For example, the CBC should certainly be given top priority. I am talking not only here of the English service, but French service as well. In our considered opinion, that is first. Public television services should have top priority.
Number two should be the provincial educational services. For example, TV Ontario here in the province of Ontario has to be given priority consideration. Put it on the first tier, to use this fast-fading television language. After that comes, in our opinion, the Canadian privately owned services, Global, CTV, and other private services.
After those services have been given first priority on the television system-CBC, provincial educational services and the private Canadian services-then the rest can come, be it specialty services, American services, community channels, whatever.
I perhaps failed to mention that we feel that community access channels or community access services should be given a major priority at the top of the channel. There is no doubt about it, if a service shows up on those first channels, on those beginning channels, say channels 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10, they are going to be watched more. They are going to be exposed more, if I can use that word, to the viewing public than those channels that may be up at 30,40 and 50. At least that is the kind of thinking that I would have on that.
As I said in my beginning words, priority at one time was not a big deal in television because there were only one or two services. That is not the case any more. We as parliamentarians have to make sure these priority services are given top treatment, first treatment.

Mr. Speaker, if you look at this particular amendment and all the amendments brought forward by my colleague, it is merely a matter of the line on which the amendment is to be completed, because we would certainly not, in any sense of the word, wish to remove the carriage of local Canadian stations. Therefore the numbering on the line was inaccurate. All we have asked for in this amendment is instead of lines 12 to 14, just line 12. It has nothing to do with the content of the wording whatsoever.
What we are really talking about is empowering the CRTC in this bill which, in a sense, is defining the relationship between the regulator and the body politic. That is really what we are talking about.
We are saying that all elements must collaborate, must work together, and play a role in ensuring that the Canadian broadcasting system and its Canadian content be a reflection of this particular act, which is the Canadian Broadcasting Act.
One of the ways that we can ensure the appropriate application of a Canadian Broadcasting Act is to ensure that this system works effectively and efficiently, and that we ensure windows or accesses so that the public can see what is on that screen.
In amendment 30, I had addressed the issue of ensuring that the CRTC, as the regulator, would have the responsibility for applying the principle of an orderly and organized Canadian broadcasting system. In this particular amendment, I am ensuring, hopefully, that the distribution undertaking -that is the cable company-will similarly have that responsibility.

December 3, 1990

I am very sensitive to the fact-that a nation that overly restricts its citizens access to information and to entertainment could not be considered or claim to be a free society. Certainly we know all about that. We have seen the walls crumble in those societies that have not allowed ordinary citizens to have access to information, education and programming.
On the other hand, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that a nation that relinquishes control over its communications policy to extra-territorial forces will ultimately cede its sovereignty as well over much of its affairs.
I know that this minister has been very sensitive in many, many areas to the concerns of artistic integrity, artistic merit, and artistic productivity in the field of the arts within our society, particularly to those who are writers, singers, performers and certainly those who can prepare the scenarios that appear on film on our screens, either on video or in the theatres. So I find it quite surprising that the holes in this bill allow for much more Americanization than I believe this minister was prepared to allow in the first place. Whether that is a fallout from free trade or something else, I am not sure. But, as there is no more pervasive medium than that of broadcasting to ensure enlightenment, entertainment and information, and no more powerful way of getting one's message across, I wonder if the minister realized the impact of first of all not ensuring that all programs that appear on our cable need to have a sanction and go through the CRTC.
There are marvellous ways in which the CRTC through article 9.4 can exempt, but everything that goes on that screen should be under the charge of the regulator. It should not be up to the cable operators to decide what and who shall get onto our screens, but it should be brought before the regulator for permission.
I would like to point out that at the present time the majority of the programs that are heard are from sources outside of Canada. It has been emphasized to us time and time again that continued reception of these has a tendency to mould the minds of young people to ideas and opinions that are not necessarily Canadian. We saw
that happening through the kind of broadcasting and the input into China and Tiananmen Square and we saw, when access was closed down, what happened.
We saw what happened in Berlin with the newly emerging democracy. It was hit constantly by the Voice of America, by Radio Canada International and the BBC, and the spark of man's normal wish for freedom of expression and freedom of action comes through when a role model is seen. The Canadian role model is different from the role models one might see in Britain, in France, or in the United States, our largest cousin to the south. Although there is nothing wrong with the United States, it is a different country. I think we want to maintain who we are and what we are. When we consider this medium and the geographic dimensions of Canada which are enormous, broadcasting can be that great force in fostering that national spirit and interpreting national citizenship and leading to national unity.
Given that an average of 10,000 hours of mostly American television are watched by our children as they grow up it is vital, in the national interest, to ensure access to a larger percentage of those 10,000 hours as Canadian. This does not mean to say that one should close his eyes or ears to the rest of the world. What it is saying is to affirm and reaffirm our future through the presentation of those kinds of information and entertainment that tells the story of who we are no matter on which coast of the three we live.
I would say that our national realities in both taste and in culture are properly reflected and accessible when our programming and the operations of our Canadian broadcasting system are in conformity and cable has the responsibility, as much as broadcasters, to ensure that we get access to that kind of programming.
I have indicated in Motion No. 24 that I want to see us put an orderly process within our regulatory structures so that our cable priority rankings would include the publicly-mandated services, which would include the public educators as well and followed by those independent educational authorities, we would have the private sector and the local level, following of course the retention of the three plus one, PBS, ABC, NBC and CBS.
December 3, 1990

Those are important. Then you add on above that, Mr. Speaker, anything else that is deemed through consultation and the regulator as advisable.
Mr. Speaker, I say to you that if we do not make affordable and accessible to the general population through cable the kinds of programs I am talking about and you allow complete access to anything, we make a big mistake.
Cable rates are going up. People do not have options and choices on those cable rates. If the cable people are not careful and do not pay attention, and if the regulator does not pay attention, we are going to be in a serious dilemma. Then we will need to have a serious public debate.
Shall we open up cable so that we can have an open Sesame situation where cable shall have competition? Or, shall we look at them as public utilities and regulate them like we do Bell Canada and our telephone companies? Is that what cable wants?
There is a serious concern about the profits. There is a new thing out there that is not even addressed in this bill which is very disquieting. It is called Skypix. I do not have the time to talk about this incredible United States satellite service that is coming in and is going to block every single window and for which we are going to have a problem.
I just want to put on record-this will be the last point-that Statistics Canada gave us some extraordinary figures with respect to the Canadian communications industry.
In 1988, the gross revenue for Canadian cable companies was just over $1.2 billion. During the same year, the gross revenue of all Canadian radio and television stations was just under $1.2 billion. The after tax profit for cable was $173 million and for broadcasters $77 million.
In 1989,-look at the change-when cable's after tax profit rose to $218 million, broadcasters' after tax profits declined to $51 million. I would suggest that in these circumstances it is ironic that the CRTC continues to look to broadcasters for the most stringent requirements to provide support for our cultural and industrial policy objectives and the cable people have only the responsibility for the community channel.

I would like to strongly recommend that we support Motion No. 24, for organization; Motion No. 25 on foreign services and Motion No. 27 that would look at cable rates. I think then we would do a good job for the Canadian broadcasting system.
