Mr. Speaker, I want to deal specifically with Motion No. 34 in this particular grouping of motions and talk about the proposed reorganization of the CRTC.
We on this side of the House feel very strongly about this, because the ultimate effect of this part of the bill will be to balkanize the CRTC: balkanize, break it up and render it unable to give a real national pan-Canadian focus and views to its decisions.
We have said many times that this government is dangerous. It has, in a very systematic way, begun to destroy the traditions of the country, to destroy the institutions of the country, to break apart the very fabric of this country and to undermine the very foundations of this country. We see it in this bill; we see it in spades.
Up until now the CRTC could take a pan-Canadian view. It could take a very wide perspective of this country because its decisions had to reflect the entire body, that is the entire commission. If Bill C-40 goes through, that will not be the case any more. The effect of this bill will be to to break up CRTC into panels and to turn each little panel into its own fiefdom. That is what will happen.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, if you have a panel for Atlantic Canada, a panel for the province of Quebec, a panel for Ontario, a panel for the prairies, and perhaps a panel for British Columbia? You are going to have a panel of the CRTC for each region of the country. How is it possible that over a long period of time those panels are going to employ, exhibit and express a consistent point of view? It is impossible. It is inevitable that they will reflect their own regions. Over a period of time you will find an inconsistency in the opinions and decisions of the CRTC.
That is not good for this country. It is certainly not good for the unity of this country. Somebody has to speak for the country. Somebody has to render decisions that have a pan-Canadian view. The CRTC is an absolutely, crucial, important institution. If the CRTC is going to be balkanized, if it is going to be broken up, that is going to hurt this country. It is going to hurt national unity. We already have enough disunity in this country as a result of this government's policies. I am sure there are some people, certainly the Conservatives on that side and some viewers would say that this is just a partisan view, this is just a Liberal speaking, this is just the opposition speaking. After all, the opposition could never find anything good about what the Tories put forward so they have to find something wrong with almost every part of the bill.
You've got that right.

The Minister of Transport says that I have it right.

Let me read some comments. This is what Mr. Spicer, now the head of the Citizens Forum said on February 22 of this year:
I do not think "they who hear decide" at all helps strengthen the national will or the national identity. It can be argued that, psychologically, if you make the regions feel more secure or powerful, and they are doing things for themselves, this in itself makes them accept the country more. Mr. Speaker, I mentioned the name Patrick Watson a moment ago. Maybe I should not have said that. I do not have a quote of his so I will withdraw that reference to Mr. Watson.
In summation, this is a bad precedent, a terrible mistake, and I think we are going to pay for this mistake in the years to come. It is about time that we started giving more consideration to this whole country. We have become too parochial. We have become too provincial. We have become too regional. Somebody has to offer a Canadian perspective. If we do not, if we withdraw, if we go back into our regions and if we only express those things which we deem important for the regions, for our own narrow turfs, if I can put it that way, that is going to harm this country irreparably.
I would hope that the government would come to its senses and withdraw this aspect of the bill because it will serve no good. It will not serve broadcasting in a positive way, Mr. Speaker. What I would like to see are those issues which the chairman deems important.
I think that under the Broadcasting Act the chairman of the CRTC should be able to deem certain issues of national importance and that decisions made concerning those issues cannot be made by panels but only by the full body of the CRTC. That would give the chairman more power and give him or her the opportunity to say to the CRTC that we, in this particular case, are going to render a national decision, a decision with a national perspective, with a pan-Canadian view.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on behalf of my colleague, the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam who has moved Motion No. 32.
I should point out before I begin that it was unfortunate in the previous proceedings of the House that when I understood the amendment to Motion No. 24 was being
Government Orders
presented, it was to be voted on separately. I did not understand at the time that having voted on the amending motion, in fact the whole group would be voted on. Unfortunately, I did not get an opportunity to speak to Motions Nos. 27 and 28, which have also been submitted by my colleague, but because the motions are reflected in Motion No. 32,1 think the comments will be pertinent to all of those motions described.
The amendment basically establishes or provides assurance that there will be efficient delivery of programming in the cable industry at rates that are at all times justifiable and reasonable. I want to point out that the cable industry is the only territorial monopoly whose profits are unregulated.
In the opinion of many, the cable industry has been a virtual licence to print money. This amendment, along with others, would apply the same kinds of pricing rules to cable companies to establish sensibility and sensitivity in pricing that have been established in other jurisdictions, for example, to telephone companies under the Railway Act.
The Railway Act states that all tolls must be "just and reasonable". Just and reasonable has been, I submit, interpreted to mean that the rates must be profit regulated. The cable industry earns on the average close to 30 per cent profit on its fixed net assets according to the 1989 commission, and in our judgment the appropriate rate of return for this industry should be closer to the 16 per cent range on net fixed assets. This would be roughly equivalent to Bell Telephone's range of 12.25 per cent to 13.25 per cent profit on average common equity.
The cable industry's profits are very healthy indeed. I think these amendments would ensure that there is not the kind of price gouging which can take place in an industry that remains as yet completely unregulated. Cable rates have risen astronomically in Canada in recent years. Cable increases averaged about 6 per cent a year between 1984 and 1988. They rose 29 per cent in the 18 months since 1989, a 29 per cent increase in their rate structures. That is a pretty significant wallop in the pocketbooks of consumers in Canada. It has occurred at a time when average telephone rates in Canada have actually been on the decline. As a result, consumers of

December 3, 1990
Government Orders
monopoly cable services have been left virtually unprotected from these excessive price increases.
Telephone rates are just and reasonable, as I mentioned before, because the Railway Act, in fact, says they have to be. It specifically instructs the regulator to enforce rate of return provisions. It is in the legislation. In contrast, the CRTC presently has full discretion in setting cable rates and the result of this has been very plain to see. As I mentioned, there has been a 29 per cent increase in rates in the past 18 months.
Given that Canadians pay over $1 billion annually in cable fees, they would be interested to know just how rates are set by the commission. Before 1986, the main criteria used by the commission in setting rates was how much other cable companies were charging in the same general area.
The Public Interest Advocacy Centre has pointed out that this meant the greediest or the least efficient operators would apply first for a rate increase and then others would follow shortly. That has been the situation.
In effect, less efficient systems were used by the larger ones as an excuse to overcharge Canadian consumers. In 1986, a new formula was developed by the CRTC. Cable companies were given automatic increases of 80 per cent of the Consumer Price Index increase, plus an additional increase to cover the cost of capital investment in the system, an extraordinary increase based on need.
This formula was modified in May of 1990, but it remains basically intact.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure where I was, but I will try to get back to where I left off.
I think the argument I was making, at the time when I was interrupted by a point of order, was that the cable industry in Canada is a virtual monopoly. Canadians cannot simply go out and start their own cable company business to compete with one that is already established. If consumers are unhappy with the service of their local cable company, they cannot switch companies because there is only one cable company serving that particular neighbourhood. They are stuck. It is as simple as that. Moreover, notwithstanding the claims of cable operators, other technologies such as satellite dishes and so forth are effectively beyond the reach of most Canadians. They are simply too expensive to consider putting in for a single network.
The Public Interest Advocacy Centre stated some time ago, before the legislative committee, that "approximately 80 per cent of households subscribe where cable TV is, in fact, available, usually in urban areas. This high rate of penetration is not affected significantly by the income level of subscribers. Households below the poverty line allocate a relatively large portion of their income for receiving cable TV services." The reason is

Government Orders
simple. The quote continues: "Cable TV provides the only form of entertainment that is remotely within the reach of low income Canadians."
It is significant that we have, in Canada, a situation which is allowed to be an unregulated monopoly in the cable industry. It is a situation which I have mentioned before. It has shown dramatic price increases of 29 per cent in the last 18 months alone. I think that speaks very clearly that there needs to be some form of regulatory authority in determining the rate structure for cable TV services.
The amendments that my colleague from Port Moody-Coquitlam proposed merely seek to provide cable subscribers with some form of fairness. It seeks to limit, to a degree, the profits of a monopoly industry and ensure that Canadians will get a much deserved break in their cable bills. The amendments would ensure that companies applied for rate increases only on the basis of a legitimate financial need. This is the same standard, I might add, that is applied to telephone companies and other monopolies.
Profit regulation has not denied the telephone or pipeline companies from making a fair profit. It has not undermined the investment in the system and, indeed, Canada has retained one of the finest telecommunication systems in the world.
Let me conclude by saying that the amendments proposed would simply provide the appropriate basis for setting cable rates in the future so that consumers, as well as the cable operators, are protected by a system that is both fair and equitable.

Mr. Speaker, what we are dealing with in this section of the bill is essentially the Balkanization or the regionalization of the CRTC.
What we had before was known as "they who hear decide". In the past, we have established, through the CRTC, the reputation of fair regulator, an intelligent regulator, and one that has a good solid record of being connected with a common view across this land.
I had a letter that came from TVA in which TVA pointed out that it had had some experience internationally. The way in which regulation is handled in France is
something of serious concern, and we would not want something such as that to happen here. I will come back to that perhaps a little later in this debate.
Right now, we are talking about no longer requiring the taking of decisions in the national interest. We are going to take an approach rather than the collegial one, where a panel may have gone out, heard, come to a conclusion, and came back to the executive committee, reported the hearings and the views, concerns and considerations and gave a recommendation. The executive of the CRTC would then put this into balance with everything that had been happening across the country. In this way, there was a potential for a less fragmented policy, and we would certainly have more even and fairer decision making across this land.
This particular issue has been one of serious concern. Many witnesses appeared before the committee and spoke at great length and from depth of heart about the disintegration of a national regulator through this kind of a process called panels of "he who hears decides". Of course, in the changing dynamics that is Canada today, it becomes all the more sensitive to have these kinds of decisions that may be irregular across this land and may not always be in the best interests of all Canadians, of both language groups and of minority status across the land.
One of the things that caused some reaction was a decision to award a new country music FM radio station in Toronto. There was a difference of point of view between the panellists and the regulators on the executive committee. There was some feeling that perhaps the black dance group ought to have received the mandate, rather than the country music format. The merits of the case were what the cabinet reviewed.
We now see that there was a frequency available and the case presented before the CRTC was a case that was offering incredible benefits to Canadian country music and artists. They are prepared to expend $800,000 a year on developing and promoting Canadian country music, with special emphasis on local performers and on radio programs and events. That is more than double what any other station in the market spends on talent development.
December 3, 1990

Certainly the Minister of Communications has been very sensitive to the development of musical talent in the country, the recording industry, and the distribution of Canadian songs. He should feel very comforted when he sees something of this nature. They made a commitment that 32 per cent of the new station's play list in the first year of operation will be Canadian content, rising to 40 per cent in the fifth year.
These proportions are very stunning if you realize that we have had between 20 and 30 per cent. On the French side, we had to have a big battle. We had to put money in and have sorts of support mechanisms and measures to ensure that the French song industry survived and grew, all the while knowing that we have fabulous artists and talent out there.
There were other things that were being done by that group that allowed them to win this particular request for a radio station. It is regrettable. There is a new frequency opening and new decisions will be made. I hope that the multi-racial, multicultural reality of Canada will be further reflected on our air waves when this new channel comes up. Notwithstanding, fair is fair, and one has to follow the rule of the commitments that were asked for by the CRTC.
With this "he who hears decides", when the idea of a resident regional commissioner is combined with those "who hears decides", one runs the risk of creating fiefdoms across the country and capturing the local industry. I quote Mr. Keith Spicer, who stated: "In broadcasting you have to look at the whole matrix of issues, many of them very subtle cultural issues, and I mean regional cultural issues. It is not only a matter of law, it is a matter of common sense sensitivity, as well as law. That is why in the broadcasting area, we think it is much better to have one national consensus so we can compare what we are doing in Newfoundland and Saskatchewan, and make sure that all Canadians feel they are being treated the same way recognizing their differences. At a time when there are some regional inter-ethnic tensions in Canada, we ought to be looking for some of these mechanisms to have a strong national view, but with much greater sensitivity to regional concerns. We all know that it is like squaring a circle but that is what we are trying to do and in our honest opinion, we think it could occur and be better done that way, rather than applying the "he who hears decides."
Government Orders
There was no question that Wick Communications felt that the principle was wrong. It was a destabilizing policy. There would be inconsistent results coming out of this. CFCF stated that it runs the risk of contradicting one of the fundamental objectives of the system to maintain a single system. TV Ontario said the regionalization of the commission and the initiation of the "he who hears decides" rule will lead to fragmentation of national policy and a general confusion as to the guiding principles of regulations in all parts of the country. The CRTC in its brief to the legislative committee on February 22 made an impassioned statement with respect to what it felt would be an ineffective and very improper approach.
I forgot to mention that Rogers believes that one of the overriding strengths of the CRTC since its establishment has been its ability to bring a broad range of national and regional concerns to bear on its decisionmaking. It felt it was very important, and were very deeply concerned that a more decentralized structure, even with the provisions requiring informal consultation, will result in the loss of this national dimension in the decision-making process. As a result, policies could diverge from region to region. We have heard from many with respect to this.
The commission, which has had experience in this particular regard with both the collegial and the small task forces, has made it very clear that basically, in a cultural industry and cultural regulation, one has to recognize that in the broadcasting industry, being an evolving one, highly sensitive and complex, decisions must be taken in full awareness of its impact on the entire system. Decisions involving individual licencees should find their anchor in and be consistent with a national overview.
There are many other aspects that the CRTC addressed; the fact that they have fact-finding bodies, the fact that it makes little sense when applied to a body whose function it is to apply a parliamentary policy in order to ensure that the cultural identity of a nation is preserved and strengthened. In broadcasting matters generally facts are seldom at issue. It is the consequences which flow from those facts which must be determined.
In closing, I would like to read into the record what the Canadian Bar Association, Media and Communication Law Section said, because they really are the experts, as well as the CRTC in this matter. They said: "We believe that the decision should not be required to be made by an ad hoc panel sitting in a particular city, rather where the commission deems it appropriate, it should be

December 3, 1990
Government Orders
possible under the act for such matters to be discussed and determined on a collegial basis in that by the full commission based on their collective experience. While it is true that a hearing panel could consult with the commission staff or with other commissioners pursuant to subsection 19(4), we believe that rule-making proceedings of this kind should involve the full commission".
I sincerely hope that the minister will look at this favourably and consider adopting an amendment called for by all sectors in this field.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. The motion reads:
That Bill C-40 be amended by deleting Clause 28.
In this legislation the government has taken a new power vis-^a-vis the CRTC, namely the broad power of policy direction. This allows the government to provide leadership and direction in broadcasting from time to time.
The power of policy direction was in fact recommended by many committees on broadcasting and we fully support it. At the same time, the government kept its power to review every CRTC decision. The various committee reports recommended that if the government took the power of policy direction, it should in fact give up its power of review. In fact, this joint power seriously tilts, we submit, the delicate balance between the government and the regulator too strongly in favour of the government.
It risks undermining the independence of the commission and as a result we have moved this motion to delete the power of review. In support of this motion, I would ask the consideration of the House. I think the concern is a legitimate one. I ask the government to consider the overwhelming view of the witnesses that were called before the committee and accept the amendment standing in the name of the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this motion. I will make my comments brief because I know I have the undivided attention of the minister across the way who is listening attentively to my remarks, and will no doubt reconsider what his position on this issue is in light of what I am about to say. speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-40 would jeopardize the CRTC's ability to carry out its role as an expert independent quasi-judicial body because it would grant a new power to the Governor in Council while retaining the existing one. Basically, it would permit the cabinet to issue policy directions to the CRTC, but it would retain its ability to set aside decisions of the commission on the basis that the decisions derogate from the attainment of objectives of the broadcasting policy.
These dual powers of cabinet in the view of our party, that is the power of review over the CRTC and the power to establish the general policy directions of the CRTC, are quite excessive. We believe that our cabinet review should be removed and in that way the government- and I say this for the benefit of the minister across the way-will ensure, or at least we believe it would assist greatly, in ridding the uninvited political interference that could perhaps jeopardize the independence of the commission.
I wonder if the minister is aware that the Friends of Canadian Broadcasting in their brief to the legislative committee said that the cabinet review powers would "undermine the independence of the CRTC in licensing matters, opens the way for policy political interference, and encourages licensees and applicants to bypass the CRTC if they think politically directed appeals will be more cogent."
What this means of course-and I say this to the minister across the way-is he is creating a situation whereby he is going to invite lobbyists from all over the place to his office. I challenge the minister: does he want to see the Frank Moores of this world and all those people all over his office? Would you want that, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
December 3, 1990
Government Orders
Speaker? I do not think I would. I think the member for Mount Royal, were she at this moment the Minister of Communications-which she will be after the next election, of course-she would not want that kind of proposition.
Let the minister think for a moment of the next government, the next Liberal government, which is going to be charged with straightening things out after they are finished messing things up, is going to want to have this bill done properly. I say to the minister, you might as well fix this now, pursuant to recommendations that we are making on this side of the Etouse.

I would like to read a few more quotes. The Canadian Institute of Adult Education had this to say: "The power of review threatens the independence of the CRTC because, apart from dictating to the CRTC- its major directions- the government will also prescribe the procedures for implementing its own policies." Thus the government defines the operating policy of the CRTC then, of course, it also has the power to take a second look after each case is completed.
In other words, the government acts as if it was itself some kind of a CRTC by taking away many of its powers, thus opening the door to the lobbyists.
[English)
Finally, I would like to read a quote from ACTRA: The power to review should be removed.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the minister will now be convinced to correct the wrong of his previous views and to straighten things out pursuant to the recommendation which I make to him now on behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal Party.

Mr. Speaker, this is quite a simple matter. We are just talking about removing ministers and the cabinet. In this particular article the powers that are being accorded the Governor in Council allows for interference, favouritism, and cronyism. It is very unhealthy. Ministers across the way must recognize by now that that is very unhealthy. Why
subject themselves to the potential for pressure where it is unnecessary?
I have said to the minister's face that he has done a good job with this bill, except for the few significant errors in here which make it an untenable bill. In general, if he would change a few little things, four little amendments, he would have a good bill. This is one of the four.
Perhaps the minister did not think it through and would like to change his mind. His parliamentary secretary has been incredible. I am sure the Minister of Communications recognizes the role his parliamentary secretary has played in carrying the ball with this bill for such a long time. In this particular section the minister gives the power of direction to the regulator. I think it is an excellent idea. After all, Parliament should decide how this very sensitive instrument of public policy should work.
Once the government decides and directs, then it is up to the CRTC to hold the hearings, to have the parliamentary committees do the listening, and to come back with an answer. That answer should not then be subject to review by cabinet. It is a very dangerous precedent.
If it is to be subject to review by cabinet, I hope, while the minister does not seem to be constraining himself or his cabinet, that he will at least make sure that this is a very narrow power of review. I happen to think that it is a very bad power of review and that is why my colleague, the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, and I have called for this particular removal.
This is essentially the bottom line as far as I am concerned. Serge Gouin, president and chief executive officer of Tele-Metropole, points out how important and detrimental the power of review can be. He says something very interesting which perhaps we would all like to know. Tele-Metropole is the largest television broadcaster in Quebec. It owns, as we all know, CFTM, channel 10 in Montreal, CJPM-TV in Chicoutimi, and numerous other subsidiaries producing films and videos. It has over 1,000 employees. It employs 2,000 people on a temporary basis, and it has the highest viewing time per week in Canada. This is a competent, well managed,
December 3, 1990

forceful and innovative broadcaster who knows what he is talking about.
In talking about the CRTC and the impact of these two powers at both ends, this broadcaster wrote:
I am one of the few Canadians to have been through the experience of obtaining an operating licence for a television network abroad and I am certainly the only Canadian to have done so in France.
That is up to the time that he wrote this. He goes on to write:
I played a very active part in the project for the privatization of TF-1 and in the issuing of operating licences for two national channels, La Cinq and M-6. In addition, I am one of the three shareholders who appeared before the CNCL, the equivalent of the CRTC in France, to obtain the licence for La Cinq.
The CNCL was established relatively recently, and at that time the French government indicated that it fully intended to ensure the independence of the organization by means of clear, precise regulations. Despite that statement of principle, the door remained open to political interference and this did not take long to materialize.
Consequently, no procedural rules established by the CNCL were taken seriously and even the conditions opposed when operating licences were issued are openly flouted today. Eighteen months after the decisions were handed down on these three national channels, a number of people are still contesting these decisions and making representations to the political authorities in order to reopen the cases even though they resulted in investments of hundreds of millions of dollars.
We know that it takes that kind of money to prepare and to be ready. What he is bringing to our attention, and I think wisely, to try to save us a lot of heartache, is that through this bill we in Canada are preparing to create the same climate, with all the consequences that one could have easily observed if one had examined the impact of such policies in other countries.
I suggest to the minister and to the Governor in Council that before they take the vote on this amendment they should listen to Tele-Metropole and its experience. They should listen to the people who appeared before us. They should listen to the report that goes as far back as the Aird report in 1928 when it talked about the independence of the government of the day and ensuring that no political pressures could be exerted. It asked that we weigh arguments dispassionately through this arm's length regulator so that we would not have the parochial political pressures which are inevitable when big money and big businesses are involved this way.
Government Orders
I hope they will protect the ministers and the arm's length aspect. I also hope they will stay out of both power direction and power review. These tandem powers are very dangerous.

Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate we have quite successfully made efforts to show where the government has made some serious errors, where it has been quite misguided in the crafting of this bill.
When it comes to the dual powers that this bill proposes to give to the government, it really smacks of a power hungry government which says that it is not good enough to have just the power of direction over the CRTC but that it must also have the power of review.
In effect the government is saying that it will tell the CRTC what to do, that the CRTC will go out and do its job, but that if it has second thoughts, or if in its opinion the so-called arm's length independent commission does not do a very good job, it will have the power of review and it will correct the mistakes.
It is a major mistake. This is a blunder of the first rank of this government, to take unto itself both the power of direction and the power of review. It makes no sense whatsoever.
In a way it suggests that the government is politically masochistic. It really wants to injure and bring grief to itself, because we can imagine what will happen if there are parties out there in the broadcast field who know that if the CRTC renders a decision they do not like the government has the power of review. What will they do? I am talking about the parties now. In effect they will ignore the decision of the CRTC. They will bypass the CRTC and go to the political headmasters at the top to appeal or argue before the government that the CRTC has made a terrible decision that is not in the national interests and certainly not in their interest. They will ask the politicians to review this decision and change it in their interest.
It makes no sense whatsoever, unless you are a government that is power hungry, wants to have control over every facet of the process and really does not respect for one minute the independence of the CRTC.

December 3, 1990
Government Orders
We must have a commission that we have faith in and that we respect, one that we feel has some competence. Sure, the government has the responsibility to set down broad policy and to give direction. There is nothing wrong with that whatsoever. It is a way of saying that the democratically elected people rule, but surely the power of direction is enough.
What more do they want? Having the responsibility and the power to set policy, to set direction, and then to say to these people who comprise the CRTC "go ahead and do your job within the ambit of the directions that we give you", is that not enough? I would think that is enough.
I talked about political masochism earlier. As part and parcel of that, we talk about and are concerned about political interference. There is enough political interference, as it is, in this whole business of governing a country. One will never stop political interference, but surely we do not go out to invite it; surely we do not go out and ask for political interference.
Yet, this section of the bill does exactly that. You can interfere with this commission because it does not have to be taken that seriously. After all, its decisions are not final. You can make an end run around it. You can bypass it. Or, if you do not like to think of it that way, you can indulge in some political interference, talk to the people whom you know and exercise some political muscle; you can interfere with what should be a process that cannot be easily violated. This is a serious mistake. This government does not need dual powers. It does not need both policy direction and review. One is enough.
We have looked at this bill from a to z. We have explored it very well. When it came to this part which was studied over and over again, we came to the conclusion that the government does not need both powers. The government does not need direction and review. Direction is enough. The government does not have to go any further than that to do a good job.
My esteemed colleague from Montreal pointed out earlier that a number of respected people in this country also agree with us on this side that to ask for this is dangerous government practice.
I do not know how much time I have left. Perhaps I have just a minute or two, but I want to refer to a statement made by the Friends of Canadian Broadcasting. What it has done is buttress our argument; it has given support to our arguments. The Friends of Canadian Broadcasting made a statement in its brief to the legislative committee which at that particular time was studying the power of review on the part of the government. The Friends of Canadian Broadcasting said "that the cabinet review power undermines the independence of the CRTC in licensing matters, opens the way for political interference, and encourages licensees and applicants to bypass the CRTC if they think politically directed appeals will be more cogent".
There it is in just a few words. The Friends of Canadian Broadcasting put it in a nutshell. They have summarized what I have tried to say in the last eight or nine minutes.
I really wish that the government would re-examine this part of the bill and take a good look at it. If the government really tried to be objective, it would come to one decision, that all it needs is the power of direction. It does not need also the power of review. It does not need dual powers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lyle Dean MacWilliam (for Mr. Waddell) moved:
speechtext:
December 3, 1990

Motion No. 40
That Bill C-40 be amended by deleting Clause 45.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion submitted by my colleague from Port Moody-Coquitlam states that Bill C-40 be amended by deleting Clause 45. That clause is the government's proposal to divide the CBC board into English and French standing committees.
I want to point out that we oppose this proposal and are moving its deletion through this amendment for two reasons. First, the CBC itself has strongly opposed this measure. It views it as a direct interference in its affairs and also as being potentially divisive. In its brief, the CBC stated the following:
This section provides that the CBC's Board of Directors "shall establish a standing committee of directors on English language broadcasting and a standing committee of directors on French language broadcasting, each consisting of the Chairperson, the President and such other directors as the Board may appoint".
In its submission to the Committee formed to study Bill C-136, the Corporation noted its objections to this provision and wishes now to reiterate them. In Section 3(1)(1) of the Bill, the Corporation is called upon to serve the interests of all Canadians, by reflecting Canada and its regions and contributing to shared national consciousness and identity.
In our view, the creation of such committees would run counter to the spirit of those objectives and, as well, counter to the programming independence provided in Section 44(4). We believe it should be left to 1he Board of the CBC to determine the most appropriate means of meeting the goals set for the CBC and that this provision of Section 43 of the Bill represents an infringement of that necessary freedom. Further, we feel that the exercise of responsibility for French and English language programming by these committees would run counter to the proper responsibilities of the Board as a whole. Accordingly, we make the following recommendation:
Recommendation 1: That Section 43(1), requiring the creation of standing committees of Directors on English and French language broadcasting, be deleted from the bill.
Those were the comments made in the brief by the CBC.
In carrying forth that argument, the second reason we oppose this proposal is that it is part of the government's plan to divide the CBC and to remove its role as a unifying instrument in the country.
As was said before by my colleague from Port Moody-Coquitlam, the government is meeching and leeching the CBC. First, it contends to strip the corporation's mandate to promote Canadian unity. Second, and
Government Orders
this is the subject of this motion, it divides the CBC unto itself. This, combined with its massive budget cuts of some $130 million annually over the next four years, is serving to destroy the CBC and to transform it into a public broadcaster that is essentially indistinguishable from its private sector competitors.
First, it divides the board into two standing committees. Then, it creates two corporations; one in French, the other in English. Finally, as a result of this and other policies of this government, we have two Canadas. This is what the government has been doing with VIA Rail and Petro-Canada, and now this is what it is doing with the CBC. We are committed on this side of the Flouse to fighting for a single Canada.
I want to end by quoting a recent comment in Cross Current by Stephen Godfrey. He states:
The proposed changes are a sad commentary on the fact that there remains no area in which the vety words "national unity" can be spoken without inviting attack from members of the federal government itself. There is no longer the imagination or the will to accept two concepts: that Quebec is a distinct society; and that there still might be an over-all plan and vision for the country that we still-so haltingly-refer to as one.

Mr. Speaker, that last debate warmed me up so much, I was able to remove my House leader's sweater. I can now perhaps box a little bit better with our stubborn colleagues across the floor, and they might see the light of day at least in this amendment.
We are at a time of great uncertainty in Canada, a time of division, and this is not the time to destroy the infrastructures that are in place.
With respect to the board of the CBC, any of you in this House who have ever served on a board of directors, be it of a voluntary association, a business corporation, mergers that take place, know that there is one head and they have a board of directors who have a common interest and concern in the well-being of that corporation.
As, if and when they need to address particular subjects, they split the board up according to the internal needs of that particular organization, organism, company or corporation, as the case may be. Could you give me a reason, Mr. Speaker, why within the standards and

December 3, 1990
Government Orders
norms of the functioning of an organism, one would expect a corporation of this size, having to deal with unequal balance throughout this country in French and English services-language sensitive issues-for, Mr. Speaker, you must recognize that within the English and French strata, there is not one mould.
There are French-speaking people from all over the world in this country of ours, and they are spread across the country. Whether they came from Belgian, French or North African, or Quebec stock does not matter. The same thing goes for the English constituencies. There is no homogeneity within the structures of the roles and responsibilities that this board must address.
The board of the CBC which handles radio and television in English, French and northern services that were in Inuit languages before they got cut had to be sensitive to all these issues. They had to be sensitive to the race, language and creed and try to portray the interests and concerns of Canada to the three coasts so there would be better understanding.
Now, what do you want to do? You want to take this board and divide it in half so that never the twain shall meet. They should become rubber stamps when serious financial concerns are facing this board.
Mr. Speaker, you realize that we are close to $240 million cuts within the CBC. You heard my question to the minister this morning with respect to the parliamentary channel when he made it very clear that this government, House, Parliament is not going to finance the parliamentary channel.
I invite the members opposite to take part in the debate. It will not be very long before they will not get their faces on the picture screen, because there will not be a parliamentary channel. It is not one of the mandated services of the CBC. It has other responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, you heard the debate last week on Radio Canada International at a time when we are so interested in having our values and democratic procedures explained, become part of and help what is going on in the Persian Gulf and in Iraq where the Kuwaiti and Iraqi people only hear the voice of Saddam Hussein and listen to a middle world voice like ours with a great deal of respect. No, we are going to cut that off too.
We are cutting off our nose to spite our face. The real problem is not splitting the board of the CBC. The real problem is putting some money in so that it can do the job it was mandated to do.
I refer back to a woman who I knew and admired. I think everyone in this House who knew Judy LaMarsh knew that she was a woman of great principle regardless of party or affiliation. She knew her business. She was a hard working person who was very sensitive to the country in which she lived.
She looked at the question of dividing the CBC into statutory committees. She said almost 23 years to the month, on November 1, 1967: "A statutory requirement that the board should split itself up into two would in the opinion of this government be undesirable. If the CBC is to be an instrument for the development of national unity and the continuing expression of Canadian identity, it must have a clear identity of its own that is neither English nor French, it's just plain Canadian".
Does that not make good sense? If they want to look at the problems internally, they will set up their own committees. Why should we dictate the disrupting of what is a very important structure?
Let me just tell you what Patrick Watson, speaking for the CBC board, had to say.
This is perhaps the most outstanding and strongly felt concern of
our board on the proposal that there be created a French and
English programming standing committee within the board of the

He spoke to us at committee in a very strong way saying that they disagreed, that each of those directors, whether they were French speaking or English speaking, felt that the honour conferred on them by being nominated by Order in Council through the recommendation of the Minister of Communications to the Prime Minister were there in persona for Canada. They did not come to represent a language structure, they came to represent Canadian programming, Canadian content, Canadian ingress, Canadian music, song and dance, Canadian artists, Canadian intellectual property, not to speak in a tongue dissimilar one from the other.
Gerard Veilleux said: "I do want to tell you that I do not look forward with a great deal of enthusiasm to
December 3, 1990

having to split my staff, the staff of CBC Radio-Canada. I say to you that this is very dangerous."
Keith Spicer, and these are the people who are running this public sector, said: "I spent a good part of the last 25 years working on both French and English networks and I am touched by what you say." He was answering a question I had asked him. "Personally I would not be in favour of creating two separate committees. Therefore I think that at some point, in addition to a very strong secure representation of the English and French side of things, we have to have a national view as well".
I could go on and on. I could indicate to you the cuts and the way the money is spread between the English language network and the French language network, particularly on the TV side. On the English side we have $576 million being spent, in round figures $577 million, and on the French side about $406 million. Mr. Speaker, there is not that much difference when you look at the percentage of difference of French speaking people, both in Quebec and in the rest of Canada, and English speaking people, both in Quebec and in the rest of Canada.
That is not the way you want to measure the service. You want to measure the service: "Is the program good? Is the content good? Will it sell? Is it world-class?" because that is what Canadians want and should expect.
Mr. Speaker, it is not to say there is not schlock both on the American and Canadian side. There is. But I think that CBC has a quality and a voice of its own and I think there is nothing worse that we could do than divide it up at this very sensitive time in the history of Canada.
I suggest, I recommend, I plead, I cajole, I ask the backbench, I ask the minister, speak to the minister, speak to the parliamentary secretary, get them to see the wisdom of not splitting it at this sensitive time.

Mr. Speaker, I am tempted to try again. I know there is a prohibition against referring to the absence of a member or minister from this House. I do not know whether there is a particular regulation that prevents reference to the absence of a minister's brain from this House.
As the member for Okanagan-Shuswap was talking about the issue of national unity, the hon. minister, who has demonstrated his contempt before, showed even

In this particular instance, we have another example of the fine stewardship of the government in the interests of keeping a Canadian broadcasting system. This amendment takes us back to the free trade agreement that was not supposed to touch culture. Culture was supposed to be exempt. In this particular instance, we are talking about retransmission rights that were negotiated in the free trade agreement and were given to the government through Order in Council to determine the regulations that would set the fees that were to be paid through retransmission.
I am sure that everyone in the House and in TV land knows that cable has to pay close to $50 million to American intellectual property, because we did not use a proper definition. We avoided using the definition that the Americans are using, saving themselves millions and millions of unnecessary dollars flowing out in duplicate funds.
No one wants our creative artists, our intellectual property, and the people who produce, direct, create, think, and speak for us as Canadians not to get their just due. That is not the object. Its object was to throw away our money unnecessarily and diminish our own resources, because the government was so foolish in the way it defined retransmission rights. There are two tests on retransmission. They are the grade B contour plus 30 kilometres, and whether or not there is a significant local viewing that can be received off-air. That is called the local signal. That is the American definition, and that is what we left out.
It is just a shame, because the amount that we are paying out is over twice as much as American cable systems pay for the same thing. U.S. cable systems pay
approximately 2 per cent of gross revenues to the copyright collectives. The copyright decision means for ourselves, here, that the Canadian cable systems will pay approximately 8 per cent of gross revenue to copyright holders.
It is like the spread on our money and why we have got such a growing debt. The government does not know how to manage. It is doing the same thing to our cable people, causing them all kinds of unnecessary costs.
Over 85 per cent of the money that is going out will go directly to U.S. copyright holders. Canadian copyright holders will receive only $7 million out of the $51 million collected from cable companies this year. That is going to go up. The Canadian cable consumer will eventually bear this expense. It is unfortunate that they will have to pay such a high price to the Americans in order to remit such a proportionately low amount to Canadian talent and copyright holders, because the government did such a rotten job in defining this whole bill.
I have a letter here from Mountain Cablevision, sent to me on November 26, which explains what is happening in this situation. It states, among other things, that this decision of Consumer and Corporate Affairs with respect to copyright tariffs being imposed, would have the Canadian cable industry pay almost $51 million to retransmit distant television signals to subscribers.

Tliis amount is greater than our after tax profit for the last three years, as our company is in the midst of a major system rebuild in order to improve the technical quality of the cable service we provide to our customers. Mountain Cablevision is also in the process of expanding Cable TV service to less economic and sparsely populated rural areas in our vicinity.
This burden is absolutely unacceptable:
We do not take issue with the principle of providing fair compensation to copyright holders. Do take issue with royalties which, on a per subscriber basis, will be more than double what American Cable Operators pay to retransmit distant signals.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I rose in the House on March 5, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs what steps he had taken to obtain a guarantee that, subsequent to German unification, post World War II borders between Germany and Poland would be respected.
Since that day Chancellor Kohl has offered assurances that seem to be satisfactory to Poland. For those assurances that were very important to Poland, I would like to congratulate Mr. Kohl, not only on his conciliatory position, but also on his decisive victory on Sunday, December 2 which will allow him an opportunity to see the historic unification through a successful transition.
For all the internal turmoil and economic challenge of restructuring that some experts are speculating will cost approximately $1 trillion, Germany has still offered some $13 billion of assistance to the Soviet Union this year, and is said to be ready to extend credits to Poland in context of a general framework treaty expected to be signed earlier next year.
This is all happening amidst the movement towards a new Europe of 1992. In time for Europe 1992, each east European country will be expected to get involved, to contribute, and to be an active member of the new community. For this they are going to need the support from the west.
Last week I attended a conference on the changing Soviet Union where, among other distinguished speakers, we had the honour to hear Mr. Brzezinski, a former adviser to President Carter, speak to the state of the economy of the Soviet Union. I must say that the one positive statement he had to make on the situation was on the creation of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Mr. Brzezinski felt that this was a first sign that the west was treating the economic reality of eastern Europe seriously.
Yet, Canada's commitment to the bank remains confusing. We know what the figures are in terms of our monetary contribution. We know what our contribution is in terms of our proportion of the total commitment. What we do not know is the extent of our commitment. We throw a few words and a few dollars around hoping that at least our gestures will keep the real issues at bay.
In his speech at the conference I referred to earlier, the Secretary of State for External Affairs talked about the bilateral relationship launched by the Prime Minister's visit to the Soviet Union last November. He talked of formal treaties for more co-operation. He talked of less restrictive trade agreements. He talked of environmental co-operation in the Arctic. All these initiatives have been talked about at length. In fact, that is all that has happened to date, talk and more talk about the talk.
We have yet to hear how these initiatives will come about when we face budget cutbacks to almost all our programs. We have yet to hear how they will be followed through with the limited and, in fact, decreasing budget of the Department of External Affairs.
The paradox in the government is woefully apparent when one reads the text of some of the speeches given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On one hand, he offers no real support. On the other hand, he uses, and I must add in this case, appropriate dramatic language to describe the dire needs of east European countries. In speaking about the Soviet Union at the conference, for example, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said: "The Soviet Union is at a profoundly important point. That point can be a turning point or a breaking point. Opportunity is present, but so too, is danger. It is Canada's profound interest that opportunity become accomplishment-".
Let us take the opportunity. Let us take the bull by the horns and follow through with our commitments. For a start, how about considering the suggestion made by the vice-president of Barclays Bank of Canada-U.S.S.R. Business Council's first annual meeting. Charles Attard suggests that the risks of doing business in the Soviet Union are getting worse. There is a general consensus about this statement. Instead of throwing bits and pieces here and there, let us consider joint action with the federal government and the Export Development Corporation. Make it easier for banks to invest by simply
December 3, 1990

insuring their investments. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this makes better business sense.
The problem with this government is that it lacks creativity, it lacks the political will, and its commitment is weak.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):

speechtext:
In reply to my colleague for Parkdale-High Park, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer him to page 87 of the Hansard of March 5, 1990. Not to take up the time of the House, I will not repeat what was said then, but that is where he will find the Secretary of State's reply. May I take this opportunity to remind him that the unification of the two Germanys took part on October 3. It was the happy ending to the 2 plus 4 negotiations which took place in Moscow on September 12 which brought the four powers to forego their rights over Germany and give it full sovereignty. Previously, in June 1990, the Parliaments of both the Federal Republic of Germany and the Democratic Republic of Germany had passed a resolution which recognized the existence of the Oder-Neisse border. The Minister of Foreign Affairs of Poland had taken part in the 2 plus 4 negotiations concerning the borders with Poland and the conditions connected with a treaty in that regard.
The treaty between Poland and the united Germany was signed in Warsaw on November 14. It was to be ratified in due time by both parliaments. Canada is very pleased with the conclusion of the November 14 treaty relating to the German-Polish border, as well as with the success of the German union which took place calmly, in consultation with all interested parties, including Poland and Canada, and in full respect of international law.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 29, 1990, I rose in this House to ask a question of the Minister of State for Housing regarding the federal co-operative housing program in Canada. When I rose in the House,in October to address the need for changes in the income qualification rule of the co-op program, I raised the issue of MPs such as the NDP member for Trinity-Spadina and the NDP member for Edmonton East who are living
Adjournment Debate
in federally-subsidized housing. The fact that well paid politicians are living in government-subsidized housing illustrates the urgent need for changes in the housing program.
When the non-profit co-operative housing program was introduced to Canada about 25 years ago, assistance was associated with rent-geared-to-income subsidies for low-income households who were unable to find affordable housing. Studies show that 15 per cent of Canadians must rely on some form of government assistance to meet their shelter needs. I am talking of families, of women with children, the elderly, and the handicapped who, through no fault of their own, do not have decent affordable housing. Many are paying 40, 50, 60 and even 75 per cent of their income each month for rent and heat.
There is an enormous demand for affordable housing. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation estimates that the demand for co-op units is between 164,000 and
400.000	renter households. Furthermore, there are over
40.000	names on co-op waiting lists across Canada, and co-ops have virtually no vacancies. Yet there are examples of well-to-do Canadians living in subsidized housing units, shutting out those most in need. High income earners should not be taking advantage of these funds. For example, the NDP member for Edmonton East is a resident of the Sundance Housing Co-op of Edmonton.
Sundance was given a federal cash grant of $280,000 when built and enjoys a special preferential mortgage rate of 8 per cent for 50 years, well below the current rate.
The member for Edmonton East shares the five bedroom apartment with four other people. The member's share of rent is less than $200 a month. There is a list of more than 30 people waiting to get into the Sundance development.
Does the leader of the New Democratic Party approve of her NDP members depriving lower income Canadians from much needed shelter? Would Premier Bob Rae approve? Would Bob White or Shirley Carr approve?
In Toronto, where more than 17,000 people are on lists waiting for public housing, the NDP member for Trinity-Spadina lives in subsidized housing.

December 3, 1990
Adjournment Debate
According to the research compiled in the greater Toronto area by the Ontario Ministry of Housing, an activist member of the NDP is almost nine times more likely to live in a co-op than any other renter. NDP supporters appear to take generous advantage of the very government housing programs they fight for on behalf of the poor.
Surely politicians who earn $88,000 a year, with $26,000 of that being tax-free, should not be taking advantage of the federal Co-operative Housing Program, as well as taking units away from those in greater need.
All federal members of Parliament are barred from personally participating in any federal programs. The members from Edmonton East and Trinity-Spadina, as public officials, are benefiting through low-cost housing resulting from public funds. I firmly believe that these public officials must comply with the legislation which bars federal MPs from participating in federal government programs.
Co-op housing serves low and moderate income families who cannot afford home ownership. It is deplorable that with such an obvious demand for affordable housing, politicians such as the named NDP members are taking space from the needy.
I understand that one of the arguments in favour of high income earners in the co-ops is to promote social integration. In fact, a CMHC evaluation notes:
- that co-operatives had been highly successful in achieving income-mixing without polarisation of income groups. Mixes of family types, age, race and people with various backgrounds were perceived as healthy and a strength of co-operative living.
However, I believe that this type of social integration can still be accomplished even if the high end income earners, those making over $60,000 a year, were denied occupancy in federally supported housing programs.
The latest figures show that 65 per cent of the households currently living under the co-operative program have incomes below $30,000 a year and 31.3 per cent of the households have incomes between $30,000 and $60,000. Only 3.7 per cent of the households have incomes in excess of $60,000.
The point I wish to make is that the social integration which co-op housing achieves through income-mixing
would still occur if the high-end income earners were dropped from the program. The fact is, only 3.7 per cent of the households have incomes over $60,000, hardly a substantial figure, a figure which the NDP members trying to justify their occupancy would like us to believe contributes greatly to social integration.
I am certain that by dropping high income earners from federal co-op housing programs, social integration will not be threatened. Instead, it will help alleviate the shortage of affordable housing we are facing in this country. A 40,000 name waiting list speaks for itself.
I also point out that the middle income group, those making between $30,000 and $60,000, now occupy 31.3 per cent of co-op housing and this rather high percentage would still ensure the goal of mixed income is met.
I want to make clear I am not advocating strictly low income public housing. We must get away from the concept of the old poverty ridden public housing ghettos of the 1950s and 1960s. However, there needs to be a cut-off point. Is it right to have high income earners taking away availability in co-op units from families in greater need? Surely politicians should not abuse and take advantage of a federally subsidized housing program.
I very much hope that the minister, who is going to reply shortly, will take this issue under control and bring in some type of legislation that would bar politicians at any level of government from participating in co-op development.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised a concern which is on the minds of a great many Canadians these days. The hon. member is not alone in raising this concern. Mr. Speaker, you may be aware that a great number of people have been quoted with respect to this issue. One of them, for instance, a retiree by the name of Freddie Caplan has said: "Get them out now and let the needy in".
Another resident of public housing, Gail Grieve, has been quoted as saying: "Evicting the politicians is not enough. They should be heavily fined. Retroactive back rent might be a good idea, too.
An unemployed man by the name of Mark Carter said: "Throw them out and put me in there-there's too many homeless people on the street".

December 3, 1990

Those are examples of some of the comments that have been coming to me with respect to this issue. I might say as well that 1 have also heard people suggest that even the co-op housing movement itself might be a lot better off and that there could very well be a greater groundswell of public support for co-op housing if all politicians were in fact banned from co-operative housing.
I think it is important at the same time for you, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member and all of us, all Canadians, to understand that the federal government has been formally involved now in various co-operative housing programs since 1973. Prior to 1973 there was, of course, co-op housing that was being built. It was inspired to a large extent in the maritimes by St. Francis Xavier University. At that time it was on the basis of self-help and self-financing and there was no subsidization by the public or by Canadian taxpayers.
However, since 1973 we have had three separate programs that have been assisted by the public at the federal level, two of them under the previous Liberal government and one of them under the present government. The first two generated some 45,000 or more units of co-op housing and the most recent one, some 13,000 of co-op housing. In each of those there was an income mix, as the hon. member has referred to.
In the earlier two programs, there was only a minimum of some 15 per cent of those units that were targeted for low-income people. In the present program up to 50 per cent of the units can be targeted to low income people. I am sure that the hon. member and all Canadians realize that it is very difficult to change the rules in the middle of the game for programs that have already been put in place. It is very difficult to put a ban on politicians, very difficult to enforce rules retroactively.
However, I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, and I want to assure the hon. member and all Canadians that as I go forward with recommendations to the cabinet very shortly, I will be taking all of those concerns into very serious consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased, I suppose, to be able to rise in the House and pose again a question I raised on November 21 to the Minister of Energy. However, I have to say that I am not pleased with the fact that this is probably the
Adjournment Debate
fifth or sixth time that I have raised this particular question in the House of Commons and I still do not have a satisfactory answer.
The question I asked on that date had to do with the spill of radioactive waste into Wallaston Lake about a year ago, in fact more than a year, the first week of November 1989. What happened since then has been indicative of a lot that is wrong with our whole environmental process in this country. Certainly, we still have not seen the facts come to light in this case. The reason I asked that question was because Cameco, the operating company, on that day pleaded guilty in court in Saskatoon. It changed its plea from not guilty to guilty with regard to provincial environmental charges that were laid in the province of Saskatchewan.
The reason I raise that question is, first of all, the minister turned down our request for a public inquiry, so there was no way the issues would be laid before the public in a public forum through the mechanism of an inquiry. There had been federal charges laid but the company pleaded guilty to those as well. When the company pleaded guilty to provincial charges, it meant there was no longer any mechanism whatsoever whereby the important questions that had been raised along the way could be raised again.
I did regret that day the fact that I had listened to some colleagues before whom I had raised the question of how I should pose my question. I wanted to ask, since the minister turned down an inquiry, how we get the answers to all these other questions. Instead, I asked the question in the form of these questions: Would the minister reconsider an inquiry? Of course, the minister simply said no to that, leaving the question dangling. I should have asked: How will we ever find out what was the role of the regulators in this fiasco? What impact will this industry have on northern people and their environment? Does the 1946 legislation which governs this industry have any relevance in today's world? I think those are the key questions here.
I do not particularly care how we get answers to those questions as long as we get them because, with respect to the role of the regulators, we have heard a lot said about the role of the company but very little about the role of the AECB under whose jurisdiction the inspection of this facility fell during the period of time that this whole safety system was unravelling.

December 3, 1990
Adjournment Debate
It raises a whole series of conflict of interest questions because there is a perception in this country, if not a reality, that the industry', the regulators and the government are all too close together, that there is an interchange of personnel and ideas.
I do not want to call into question the integrity of the minister. Even he is in a peculiar situation in that both Cameco, the company in this case, and the AECB, the regulator, answer to the same minister.
Then there is the question of the impact on northern people in their environment. That question has never been satisfactorily addressed although the minister indicated to the chief of the Wollaston band that it had. The chief wrote back and the minister, in fact, conceded that this huge question, which is before the Supreme Court in other forms of the role of aboriginal peoples in the control of the environment, has not been addressed.
There is the fact that we are proceeding under a 1946 act of Parliament, the Atomic Energy Control Act. Certainly technology has evolved a long, long way in our ability to monitor technology since 1946. In fact, the question remains, what are we going to do with this obsolete regulatory regime that we have in this country? The people want answers to these questions. It is not just me.
I would like to quote from the Prince Albert Daily Herald of November 28, where it states in an editorial: "Ray Funk is correct over uranium probe". This is a Thomson paper, not a house organ of my local constituency organization or anything like that. It states:
Ray Funk is absolutely correct in saying there should be a public inquiry into the safety of uranium mining in this countiy.
Funk has been pressing Energy Minister Jake Epp for the inquiry since the accident. Epp, so far, has refused, leaving Funk and many other people frustrated by the lack of answers to a number of questions.
Funk's has been a lonely voice in Ottawa on this issue. However, the MP should know he carries the support of much of his constituency, in particular its northern reaches, in this fight.
I am saying to you, Mr. Speaker, and pleading to the parliamentary secretary, through you, to please answer the questions. What is the role of the regulators? What is the impact on northern people? When will we receive new legislation on this very important industry? We need these answers. People are demanding them and I hope that the parliamentary secretary will be forthcoming.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank you for giving me this opportunity again on behalf of the government to answer the question recently raised in the House by the hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River.
As the hon. member reported, Cameco pleaded guilty on November 21 to the charge under section 17(a) of the Saskatchewan Environmental Management and Protection Act. It was alleged that Cameco had allowed the discharge of mine water without a permit in circumstances where there was a reasonable possibility that the discharge could result in a change in the water quality.
The maximum fine under this legislation is $1 million. The prosecutor for the provincial Crown recommended that a fine of $50,000 be given. The judge reserved his decision until Tuesday, November 27, 1990. On that date, the provincial court judge Albert Lavoie announced his decision to impose a fine of $50,000 on Cameco relating to the charge to which Cameco had pleaded guilty.
The hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River has repeated his call for a public inquiry into uranium mining in Canada since the prosecution of Cameco. He says that there is no longer a forum to answer the remaining questions on the issue. What question, I ask, Mr. Speaker?
The situation is very clear. It is clear that fortunately there has been no environmental damage as a result of the Rabbit Lake mine water spill. Reports prepared by Saskatchewan Environment and by Saskatchewan Research Council have each come to this conclusion, as did the Atomic Energy Control Board after it completed its investigation of the spill. The people have their answer.
The role of the regulators is clear. They investigated the incident, laid charges and followed up by reviewing their licensing and inspection practices. Follow-up action included the frequency of inspections, adding more task to the inspections such as checking the log book of the company operators and increasing the lines of communication with members of the public, especially with the natives of the Hatchet Lake band.
December 3, 1990

In addition, the Atomic Energy Control Board has recognized the need to update the 1946 Atomic Energy Control Act. As part of the revision to update this act, consideration would be given to increasing the fines and penalties to make them comparable to those in current legislation such as the federal Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
Legal procedures have made it clear that Cameco was negligent in executing certain operations related to the protection of the environment. The AECB instructed Cameco to clean up the spill; the company has spent several millions in carrying out clean-up operations. In addition, the AECB instructed the company to install a new alarm system to detect any spill of mine water and to train its staff in proper inspection practices.
With regard to the hon. member's request for a public inquiry into uranium mining, I re-emphasize that in view
Adjournment Debate
of the several public inquiries already conducted on uranium mining in Canada, of the negligible environmental impact of the Rabbit Lake spill, of the tightening of licensing and inspection practices of regulators, and of the opportunities for public input into the Environmental Assessment Review Process for any new uranium mining facilities, the government still considers that another public inquiry into uranium mining would not be in the best interest of Canada at the present time.
No, the minister has not changed his mind. [Translation]
